2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and apprised 
the Members that the Committee would be hearing the views of two Departments, namely, (i) 
Department of Atomic Energy and (ii) Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science & 
Technology on the subject, "Cancer Care Plan & Management: Prevention, Diagnosis, 
Research & Affordability of Cancer Treatment".   
3.       The Committee first heard the views of Director of Department of Atomic Energy, who 
gave a presentation, which inter alia highlighted the following points:-   
 (i) Cancer incidence in India is lower compared t o the rest of the world. In urban India 
Cancer incidence is approximately 100 per 100,000 population, and in rural India it 
stood at 45 -50 per 100,000 population. Almost two -thirds of the cancer care is 
provided in the private sector and every year approxi mately 5 per cent of the 
population went below the poverty line because of health-care related expenditure.   
(ii) Almost one-third of all cancers in India are related to tobacco in some form. Stricter 
regulations are required to regulate the consumption o f tobacco, further the sale of 
tobacco close to educational institutes should be banned. Another major cause of 
Cancer is increasing obesity amongst the Indians, the Government should take 
necessary steps to prevent rise in obesity levels.  The Government should increase 
taxes on junk food and sugary drinks as these lead to obesity, especially among 
young children.  
(iii) Two-thirds of cancers in India are diagnosed at a very advanced stage, the most cost -
effective way of reducing the burden is to do large scale screening so that early 
detection of Cancer can be ensured. Further primary care doctors and para -medical 
staff, the ASHA and Anganwadi workers, should be further sensitised and educated 
about importance of screening and early detection.  
(iv) Department of Ato mic Energy launched National Cancer Grid (NCG) in 2013 -14, 
currently, it has 266 member organisations. The aim of the Grid is to have 
standardised treatment protocols, evidence -based guidelines and a web -based expert 
opinion service.  Under Ayushman Bharat  Scheme, unless a physician adheres to the 
NCG guidelines, they do not get reimbursed under the Ayushman Bharat scheme.   
(v) Radio-pharmaceuticals developed by Bhabha Atomic Research Centre are available 
at affordable price as compared to the imported radio-pharmaceuticals.    
(vi) The hub and spoke model developed by DAE in association with Tata Memorial 
Centre is a distributed model of Cancer. In this model, Comprehensive Cancer 
Centres act as hubs and these hubs are capable of treating all cancers, including 
complicated cancer care, and up to four spokes are connected to the central hub.  
These spokes are available for giving treatment at the patient's doorstep and they are 
capable of treating more common and less complex cancers. One hub is proposed in 
every Sta te, or, per four crore population, the hub would be a 250 to 300 -bedded 
facility and the approximate capital expenditure required to set up this facility would 
be around Rs.700 crores with an annual running cost of Rs.110 to 120 crores.  On the 
other hand, a spoke is proposed for every one crore population.  The expected cancer 

230 
 
burden per spoke will be 10,000 cancer patients annually which will grow to 14,000 
by 2035.  
(vii) The Integrated Centre for Treatment, Research and Education (ICTRE) in Cancer 
having significant involvement of Ayush is being developed by DAE in association 
with Tata Memorial Centre at Khopoli near Mumbai. ICTRE will also house a state -
of-the-art clinical facility for research related to Ayush, it will also include a 
radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgery to ascertain the interactions between Ayush 
medications and the modern medicine treatment. 
(viii) Human resource required for operations in these Hubs and Spokes should be 
sanctioned at the time of project sanction as expert oncologists are not av ailable 
readily. All the hubs should have oncology degree courses to facilitate increased 
trained human resource both in the hubs and the spokes.  There is also need for 
reservation in training courses for geographically under -served areas like North -East 
India States, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh with the bond 
attached to it so that trained human resource goes back to their original States and 
serves the community.   
(ix) The Tata Memorial Center has developed an excellent model for self sustainability in 
operational expenditure, this helps in avoiding dependency on Government for funds.  
This model functions on a basis of 60:40 ratio of free to private patients.  The private 
patients pay a mark -up on their hospital bills, whereas the free pa tients are either 
completely free or at highly subsidised cost, spending only 5 -10 per cent of the total 
expenditure.    
(x) Cancer research done in the western countries is not entirely applicable to India, 
primarily because the types of cancers prevalent in India are very different from the 
types of Cancers affecting people in the western countries. The advanced treatment 
methods/ technologies developed in the West are not applicable in the Indian context 
primarily because of the costs involved, for example C AR T-Cell therapy which is a 
treatment for relapsed blood cancers costs approximately Rs. 3.5 to Rs.4 crores per 
patient if it is imported from the U.S, but the same therapy developed by Tata 
Memorial in collaboration with IIT, Bombay costs only Rs. 20 to 25 lakhs.   
(xi) There is need to increase funding for clinical cancer research.   
4.       The Committee then heard the views of the Secretary, Department of Biotechnology, 
Ministry of Science & Technology who made the following points:- 
(i) Department of Biot echnology (DBT)  supports competitive R&D programmes in 
basic, clinical and translational research, which includes research to identify different 
types of cancers, to develop nano -medicines that specifically target diagnostics and 
treatment; developing animal models for developing chemotherapeutic drugs etc; 
(ii) DBT along with Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research and Education in Cancer 
(ACTREC) helped set up International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) as India 
was one of the founding members of this ICGC; 
(iii) One of the major challenges is to set up facilities and infrastructure across the 
country. DBT has set up a cancer centre in Sher -e-Kashmir University specifically for 
diagnosis as very unique oral cancer is prevalent in Kashmir area; and 
(iv) DBT has started a major programme in cancer genomic research with National Cancer 
Institute (NCI) Centre in Jhajjar with an aim to develop personalised medicine for 
Cancer, other than this the programme focuses on early detection, establishing bio 
bank and developing animal models to analyse immune -compromised animal model 
for pre-clinical development.

3.  The Committee first heard the views of Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals,  
who in her deposition apprised the Committee that Government over the years had made 
several interventions to ensure the  affordability of cancer drugs.  The Government 
interventions included not only price regulation, but also providing drugs through public 
health services and popularizing the use of generic medicines. During the course of the 
meeting the Chairperson, National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority ( NPPA) gave a 
presentation which inter alia highlighted the following points:-   
(i) NPPA which was constituted in 1997 is mandated to implement and enforce the 
provisions of drugs (Prices Control) Order and monitor the  availability of drugs, 
identify shortages and take corrective steps wherever required; 
 (ii) NPPA is supposed to only control the price of formulations used in a drug whereas 
bulk drug prices are market driven;  
(iii) Cancer drugs are regulated under Sect ion 3 of the Essential Commodities Act and 
Standing National Committee on Medicines draws up the National List of Essential 
Medicines (NLEM) which is revised from time to time; manufacturers of non -
scheduled drugs which are not part of NLEM are free to fix  the price of a drug as per 
the cost of production but this increase in the price of a drug cannot be more than 10 
per cent in a particular year;  
 (iv) For ceiling price fixation as prescribed under the DPCO, 2013, sum of prices of brands 
having more than  1 per cent market share is taken and it is divided by the number of 
brands, to average price to the retailer 16 per cent margin is added, this gives the 
ceiling price for a particular drug;  
(v) Trade margin means the margin from the point of first sale t o the final MRP of drug 
sold to the consumer is called trade margin, para 19 of DPCO gives flexibility to 
regulate the price of drugs in extraordinary circumstances, accordingly the trade 
margin of 42 anti-cancer drugs were fixed by NPPA; 
(vi) Under Pradha n Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP), low cost generic 
Cancer drugs are made available through more than 8700 Janaushadhi Kendras, spread 
throughout the Country; the product basket has been increased to 1600 medicines and 
250 surgical items in 2021-22, the procurement of medicines under the scheme is done 
in four warehouses located at Gurugram, Chennai, Guwahati and Surat; and

legal provisions with regard to ASU drugs. Scheme of Regulation of Health Food supplements was 
transferred to the Department of Health as it comes under that Department only. The last two schemes 
at v) and vi) have been merged under the modified scheme of Drugs Quality Control to be 
implemented in the year 2005-06. 
Action Taken 
 Since the Scheme namely “Use of Modern Technology and Bio-Technology” has been shifted 
into “Extra Mural Research Scheme” of the Department of AYUSH under which, separate fund 
allocation has been made in the year 2005-06. 
Recommendations/Observations 
16.3 The Committee is constrained to note that all the above schemes were proposed to be launched 
without going into the feasibility aspect. As a resu lt, after three years two of the schemes had to be 
dropped. One was transferred to another scheme and two were merged with the main scheme of drug 
quality control. It took 3 years to realize that the subject of regulation of health food supplements 
belongs to the Department of Health as per the Allocation of Business Rules. Therefore, the Scheme 
of Health Food Supplements was transferred to the Department of Health. 
Action Taken 
 It is true that even after 3 years there wa s no proposal received under the following schemes 
such as:- 
(i) Use of Modern Technology and Bio-Technology. 
(ii) Scheme of Acquisition of ISO Quality Control Certification from ISM&H industry . 
(iii) Scheme for Introduction for A.S.U Mark and Quality Certification. 
(iv) Support for ISM&H industry for creation of labs./quality control facilities. 
(v) Assistance to Units obtaining GMP Certification. 
(vi) Regulation of Health Food Supplements. 
 During the mid-term appraisal EFC has decided to drop the above schemes from quality control 
of A.S.U. & H. drugs. Health Food Supplement scheme  has been transferred to Department of Health 
as the scheme belongs to them. 
Recommendations / Observations 
16.4 The Committee has been observing that a large number of fake herbal products and Ayurvedic 
products and medicines claiming cure for a number of  diseases are available in the open market. On a 
specific query about the quality control of AYUSH drugs, the Committe e has been informed that the 
state drug controllers are the implementing authoritie s of the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act 
and Rules thereunder. The Department has been periodically advising the state authorities to 
implement the provisions of the Act and ensure quality of the drugs. The Department has also taken a 

number of steps which include central assistance for strengthening of 21 drug testing labs of AYUSH 
system, for GMP compliance, for appointment of drug controllers/drug inspectors. 
Action Taken 
 Under the existing provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act; Chapter IV ‘A’ deals with the 
provisions of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani drugs. The enforcement of this chapter is done by State 
Drug Controller / licensing Authorities, who grant lice nses of the Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani drugs 
in their States. As for the standard guidelines, if th e ingredients of the formulation are toxic in nature, 
applicant company is required to provide safety da ta of these medicines. The Department of AYUSH 
have strengthened 23 Drug Testing Laboratories and 43 pharmacies of A.S.U. & H. drugs for 
compliance of GMP and also strengthened the enforcement mechanism in 13 States. 
XVII. EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS 
Recommendations/Observations 
17.1 There are 221 Ayurveda Colleges and 180 Homoeopathy Colleges that have the approval of 
State Governments and are by and large affiliated to the Universities. A State-wise breakup of these 
Colleges indicates that the maximum number of Ayurve da Colleges is concentrated in two States of 
Karnataka and Maharashtra. Similarly in case of Homoeopathy Colleges, Maharashtra and Madhya 
Pradesh have the highest number of Colleges. On bei ng asked about the reasons for this situation, the 
Department clarified that this was largely due to the higher degree of private initiatives in these States. 
The Central Government has been taking all preventive measures to check the mushroom growth of 
sub-standard medical Institutions of Ayurveda and Homeopathy. The Department has also informed 
that no College can be opened without a NOC from the State Government and consent of affiliation 
from the concerned University. The Committee is not fully inclined to accept the clarification given 
by the Department. The Department itself has indicated that all these Colleges are ‘by and large’ 
affiliated to Universities. 
Action Taken 
 After the Indian Medicine Central Council (Amendment) Act, 2003 and the Homoeopathy 
Central Council (Amendment) Act, 2002 came into force with effect from 7.11.2003 and 28.1.2003, 
the power of granting permission to open new Medical College, to open new higher courses of study 
or training (including Post Graduate Courses) and to increase admission capacity in the Colleges, was 
vested in the Central Government. Before the said Amendment, the Central Council of Indian 
Medicine and the Central Council of Homoeopathy, used to grant necessary permissions to the 
prospective Medical Colleges/Institutions. But after the enforcement of the said Amendment in Acts, 
the applications of the Colleges /Institutions are received in the Department of AYUSH directly. The 
applications received during the pres cribed schedule for receipt thereo f, are scrutinized thoroughly in 
the Department of AYUSH. After scrutiny of each appl ication, a copy of the same is forwarded to the 
CCIM in respect of the courses in Indian Medicine or to the CCH for courses in Homoeopathy, as the 
case may be. While doing so, the deficiencies found in the applications are indicated in the forwarding 
letters to the CCIM and CCH and copies of the same  endorsed to the applicants with the advice to 
rectify the deficiencies in consultation with the CCIM or the CCH, as the case may be. The CCIM and 
the CCH do the technical scrutiny of the applications referred to them and make their 
recommendations for disapproval or approval of the scheme in each case. The CCIM and the CCH 
depute their officers/ experts to the Colleges/Institutions for on the spot study of the infrastructure and 
facilities and minimum standards of educatio n as per the respective Regulations/Guidelines 
formulated by the Central Government. Even after the receipt of the recommendations from the CCIM 
or CCH, the Central Government may make further inquiries from the prospective Colleges and / or 
conduct visitations to the Colleges before taking decision to grant permission. 
Recommendations/Observations 

17.2 The Committee also notes that number of G overnment Colleges are very less when compared 
with the Private Colleges. Out of 221 Ayurveda Co lleges, only 54 are in the Government sector. 
Similarly, out of 180 Homoeopathy Colleges, 149 are private Colleges. This is the position in case of 
Unani and Siddha Colleges. The Committee has been informed that the Central Council of Indian 
Medicine and the Central Council of Homoeopathy made inspections of a number of Colleges during 
2002-03 and 2003-04. The Committee has been given to understand that the Colleges found lacking 
facilities for teaching and practical  training were not allowed admission. The inspection reports have 
been communicated to such Colleges for rectification of deficiencies. The Committee would like to be 
enlightened about the follow up action taken in this regard. 
Action Taken 
Compliance of deficiencies pointed out in the inspection reports is being monitored by CCIM and 
CCH as well as Government of India. Colleges which have rectified the deficiencies have been 
granted extension of recognition and others are being pursued to rectify the deficiencies to process the 
case for extension of recognition.

number of AYUSH doctors must have increased manifold in the last. three years. Prescribing 
standards of professional conduct, etiquette and code of ethics to  be observed by the AYUSH doctors 
is another important mandate of the two Councils. The Committee has been observing that at present

The Committee is of the view that there needs to be  an effective monitoring mechanism for regulating 
the AYUSH doctors practising across the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that

practice as per their State Act. However to check n on-authorised practice by unqualified/unregistered 
practitioners of ISM, the Councils placed advertisement in newspapers to generate public awareness. 
Comments of the Committee 
 Committee had drawn the attention of the Department to there being no check on practice

medicine. 
VII. CENTRAL COUNCIL FOR RESEARCH INSTITUTE OF UNANI MEDICINE, NEW 
DELHI 
Recommendations / Observations 

7.1 The Central Council for Research in Unani Medi cine, a registered society set up in 1978 has a 
network of 24 centres functioning in different parts of the country for developing and coordinating 
scientific research on different aspects of Unani Medicine. The trend of utilisation of funds during the 
first three years of Tenth Plan indicates that additional funds are being provided at R.E. stage for 
carrying out the Construction Work of Regional Research Institute of Unani Medicine, Srinagar. The 
Committee observes that during 2004-05, Plan allocation enhanced from Rs. 9.50 crore to Rs. 13.50 
crore at the R.E. stage. This add itional provision was also meant for construction of 2nd phase of the 
building of RRUM Srinagar. The Committee has been given to understand that these funds were to be 
provided to the construction wing of the Kashmir Un iversity which is constructing the building. The 
Committee finds that 2004-05 also an enhanced prov ision of Rs.11.50 crore has been proposed. The 
Committee would like to be apprised about the specific purpose for which this additional allocation is 
meant for. The Committee would also like to point out that the construction of building for RRUM has 
been continuing for about 8-10 years. The Committee would like to be enlightened about the original 
estimate and the actual expenditure on this construction project. 
Action Taken 
 It may be stated that on the request of CCRUM,  the University of Kash mir had allotted a piece 
of land in 1987 for construction of the building of the RRIUM, Srinagar. Th e CPWD could not take 
up the work in time due to disturbances in the valley. The original estimate submitted by the CPWD 
was Rs.6,08,97,000/- however the matter was considered by the Standing Finance Committee in its 
meeting held on 15.5.98 and it was desired that only modest and essential construction work to be 
taken up and revised estimate worked out then for the same was Rs.2.08 crore for the 1
st phase. 
Subsequently, the permission of University was withdrawn because of security reasons for the 
memorial of Sheikh Abdullah, facing the plot. However, on repeated persuasion, the University again 
agreed for alternative land and at that point of time in 2000, the Building Department of the University 
of Kashmir was approached for construction. Their estimates were considered by the SFC/GB of 
CCRUM, which duly approved the same and the wo rk was assigned to Construction wing of 
University of Kashmir at an estimated cost of Rs.246 lakhs in the first phase. The approval was 
conveyed to the University on 10
th May, 2001. After physically inspecting the construction activity the 
Standing Finance Committee was satisfied with the construction work in phase I and felt that 
construction work if done in total will be cheaper than if done in parts. The Committee also noted that 
phasing of the project affected some basics, such as Central Heating System, thus after noting the 
functional requirements of the Institute and keeping in view, this SFC agreed to the construction of the 
entire building as per the original plan at an total estimated expenditure of Rs.487 lakhs (It was 
Rs.6,08,97,000 as per CPWD estimates at the time or iginal plan was made). The SFC of the Council, 
therefore, approved the Second Phase of the buildi ng at an additional cost of Rs.241 lakhs (Rs.487 
lakhs total -Rs.246 lakhs released in the 1
st phase). The approval of the GB was conveyed to the 
University and an amount of Rs.437 lakhs was released to the University on this account so far. 
 It may be pertinent to mention that for 200 4-05, an initial provisioning of Rs.950 lakhs was 
suggested because at that point of time, the co nstruction of Phase-II was not included in overall 
estimates. There were some other shortages of funds in different heads of expenditure and 
provisioning for this expenditure was also to be made. Thus at R.E. stage the budget allocation was 
increased to Rs.1350 lakhs. 
 The above statement explains the position that there was no unreasonable delay. The time taken 
so far was due to disturbances in the valley and shortage of funds during previous years. 
Comments of the Committee 
 Committee’s attention has been drawn by the ve ry slow progress made in the construction 
work of the building of the Re gional Research Institute of Unani Medicine, Srinagar. The 
Committee understands that disturbances in the valley and shortage of funds are primarily 

responsible for this situation. The Committ ee is, however, not fu lly convinced by the 
justification given in this regard by the De partment. The Committee finds that not much 
progress seems to have been made in the constr uction of the building of RRIUM, Srinagar. The 
Committee had made a specific query about the orig inal estimate and the actual expenditure on 
the project. The Committee has been given to understand that against an original estimate of Rs. 
6.08 crore submitted by CPWD, total estimated expenditure now stands at Rs. 4.87 crore for the 
construction of the building undertaken by the Kashmir University. An amount of Rs. 4.37 crore 
has been released so far. The Committee’s speci fic query about the actual expenditure on the 
project remains unanswered. The Co mmittee is still not aware abou t the present status of the 
buildings of RRIUM, Srinagar. The Committee would like to be apprised in this regard.

XII. EXPANSION OF AYUSH DISPENSARIES IN CGHS 
Recommendations/Observations 
12.1 This is a new scheme started in 2003-04 for providing benefits of AYUSH system to CGHS 
beneficiaries. In its last report, the Committee had expressed its concern in the delay in the 
implementation of this scheme. The Committee observes that situation remained unchanged during 
2004-05. It has been informed that dispensaries opened in the year 2003-04 have started functioning 
and seven more dispensaries have been sanctioned during 2004-05. The Committee is, however, 
surprised to note that physical targets set during both the years i.e. 2003-04 remained unfulfilled. Not 
even one dispensary sanctioned in 2003-04 has become functional. The Committee does not have any 
hope for the seven dispensaries sanctioned in 2004-05. This is born out by the fact that allocated funds 
for the scheme remained unutilized during 2003-04 and 2004-05. The Committee is of the view that 
there is a little chance of AYUSH dispensaries sa nctioned becoming functional. The Department has 
itself conceded that there are large number of vacancies in AYUSH dispen saries. The Committee is 
not convinced by the contention of the Department that the process of new recruitment is to be taken 
up by the UPSC and revival of old posts is complicated and time consuming. The Committee is of the 
view that when the ex isting CGHS dispensaries are not fully functional for lack of AYUSH 
manpower, fate of AYUSH dispensaries proposed to be opened can be well imagined. 
Action Taken 
 Seven number of dispensaries have been sanctioned during 2003-04. Out of these the following 
dispensaries are functional: - 
 1. Trivandrum - Homoeopathic and Ayurvedic 
 2. Guwahati - Homoeopathic 
 3. Delhi - Siddha and Unani 
 The above-mentioned five units have been made functional by deployment of medical officers 
from the existing strength of the CGHS dispensaries. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is dismayed to note the very  slow progress being made in making AYUSH 
dispensaries in CGHS functional. Out of the seven dispensaries sanctioned in 2003-04, only three 
can be made functional. The Committee is not in clined to accept the claim of the Department 
that the three AYUSH dispensaries at Trivandr um , Guwahati and Delh i are now functional. 
Deployment of medical officers from the existing  strength of CGHS dispensaries can only be 
considered as a stop-gap arrangement. It seems that proce ss of new recruitment and revival of 
old posts continues to be im peded by procedural formalit ies. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should take some concrete steps to make AYUSH dispensaries 
functional at the earliest so as to increase the usage and acceptability of AYUSH system. 
XIV. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
Recommendations/Observations 
14.2 In its last Report, the Committee had commented .about the need for strengthening the Board 
with appropriate infrastructure and logistic suppor t. The Committee is, however, constrained to point 
out there has been little progress in this direction. The National Medicinal Plant Board set up in 2000, 

still continues to suffer from lack of proper infrastructure, which is essential for implementing its high 
objectives. The Committee finds that the Department of Expenditure has agreed for creation/ 
outsourcing of only 6 posts including CEO the Board. The proposal for creation of 31 other posts 
alongwith the proposal for grant of status of registered society to the Board is also under 
consideration. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the tardy progress being made in 
providing the required staff essential for its efficient functions. The Committee fails to appreciate the 
proposal of the Department of Expenditure of outs ourcing of staff for the Board. The Committee is of 
the view that there should be cr eation of all required posts. The Department should make concerted 
efforts for getting the EFC and Cabinet approval for creation of required posts at the earliest. 
Action Taken 
 Department of Expenditure has approved creation of following posts: 
1. Sr. Research Assistant - One 
2. Steno. Gr.-‘D’ - One 
3. Computer Operator - One 
Approval has also been granted by Department of Expenditure for out sourcing of following 
positions: 
1. Driver - One 
2. Messenger - One 
 An EFC note for granting autonomy to the Boar d as a registered society and sanction of 
requisite posts has been circulated to the concerned Departments for their comments before the matter 
is taken up with the Department of Expenditure. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is constrained to observe th at not much progress has been made in 2005-
06 so far with regard to creation of posts for th e National Medicinal Plant Board. Creation of 
three posts and outsourcing of three posts for the Board agreed to by the Department of 
Expenditure is yet to get the formal  sanction. Latest position in this regard is that comments of 
concerned Departments on the EFC note for sa nction of requisite posts are awaited. The 
Committee is not aware whether the Board could be made fully functional with the approved six 
posts which includes one post of  Driver and Messenger also. Th e Committee reiterates that the 
Department should expedite the process for crea tion of six posts. The Department may also 
make an assessment about the actual requirem ent of manpower for the Board and pursue the 
same with the Planning Commission-Department of Expenditure. 
XV.  STRENGTHENING  OF  PHARMACOPOEIAL  LABORATORIES 
Recommendations/Observations 
15.2 The Committee has been observing that both the labs lack required infrastructure including staff. 
The Committee observes that during the Tenth Plan Period, funds are being allocated every year to be 
reduced drastically at the RE stage, specially in the case of PLIM. The only reason cited being non-
creation of posts. The status of these labs remains unchanged for the last so many years. Year 2004-05 
was no exception. Rs. 55 lakhs were provided for PLIM, to be reduced to Rs.9.00 lakhs at the RE 
stage and the actual expenditure upto 7th March, 2005 was only Rs.4.77 lakhs. Reason given is non-
creation of posts. For strengthening of these two labs, plan allocation proposed for 2005-06 is 
Rs.150.00 lakhs. The Committee, however, strongly feels that higher allocation of funds does not have 

any meaning in the case of these labs. Lack of in frastructure is adversely affecting the achievement 
level of various physical targets set by the two labs. 
Action Taken 
 The Department appreciates the concerns expressed by the Committee. The construction of the 
building is going on in full swing and the building for HPL and PLIM are nearing completion and are 
in final stages. The proposal for creation of posts was taken up with the Department of Expenditure. 
They have raised certain queries and made certain observations. The proposal is being modified in 
view of their queries and observations. 
Recommendations/Observations 
15.3 The Committee notes that out of 36 sanctioned posts in PLIM and 32 in HPL, only 2 and 3 posts 
are lying vacant respectively. However, this strength must be based on the initial year of establishment 
of these two labs i.e in the 1970s. Since then, after more than 30 years, the requirement of posts must 
have increased manifold. The Department itself has mentioned that additional 53 posts are required in 
PLIM and 31 in HPL. As per the latest information given by the Department, for the first phase of 
strengthening the requirement of labs, 16 and 19 posts were projected for PLIM and HPL respectively. 
The matter is under the consideration of the Department of Expenditure. 
Action Taken 
 The Department appreciates the concerns expressed by the Committee. The construction of the 
building is going on in full swing and the building for HPL and PLIM are nearing completion and are 
in final stages. The proposal for creation of posts was taken up with the Department of Expenditure. 
They have raised certain queries and made certain observations. The proposal is being modified in 
view of their queries and observations. 
Recommendations/Observations 
15.4 The Committee is anguished to note that another plan period would be over and these two labs 
will continue to suffer from lack of required staff. The Committee finds that PLIM continues to 
function without a Director. Nothing can be more unsatisfactory. In view of a very large variety of 
AYUSH drugs in the open market, th ese labs have to be fully oper ational. The Committee reiterates 
that the Department should vigorously pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance and other 
authorities. 
Action Taken 
 Requisition has been sent to UPSC for filling up of the posts of Director, PLIM and HPL. The 
matter regarding creation of posts has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance. 
Recommendations/Observations 
15.5 The Committee was given to understand that buildings for HPL and PLIM are expected to be 
ready by February, 2005. However, as per the latest  information, the buildings of HPL and PLIM will 
be ready by June, 2005 and July, 2005 respectively. The Committee hopes that there would be no 
further delay due to formal clearance by Fire Department and other allied agencies. 
Action Taken 
 A meeting was held in the Department. on 30.6.2005 wherein the representatives of CPWD 
promised to handover the buildings complete in all respects with all mandatory certificates by 
October, 2005. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee views with serious concern the state of affairs in both the Labs; i.e. HPL 
and PLIM. The Committee was given to unders tand that the buildings for HPL and PLIM 

would be ready by Februa ry, 2005. However, the date for comp letion again shifted to June-July 
-2005 and as per the latest info rmation, the buildings were to be  ready in all respects with all 
mandatory certificates by October, 2005. The Committee is not aware about the latest status but 
hopes that targets must have been achieved. Also , as regards the proposal for creation of posts, 
the Committee opines that the Depa rtment should not only submit the modified proposal to the 
Department of Expenditure at the ea rliest but also pursue the same so  as to get it arrive of the 
logical conclusion. All efforts should be made to get the post of Director, PLIM and HPL filled 
up urgently. The Committee hopes that the De partment would work towards removing all 
bottlenecks in the whole process beca use the objective of these labs i.e. laying down the 
standards for drugs of AYUSH and also for their te sting/analysis is of immense importance for 
users. 
XVI. DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL 
Recommendations/Observations 
16.5 The Committee notes that only three states have responded about the availability of spurious 
drugs in their states during the last three years. In  Andhra Pradesh, samples of 25 ayurveda drugs and 
29 samples of homoeopathy medicines were analyzed. Gujarat Government has initiated action 
against one person for selling spurious Ayurvedic product. 9 samples of fake homoeopathic medicines 
were analyzed in Delhi. The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction with the scant feedback about 
spurious AYUSH drugs for such a big country and that too for a period of three years. The Committee 
would emphasize that the Department should pursue with all the departments so that 
preventive/deterrent action can be initiated, wherever required. 
Action Taken 
 Department of AYUSH have constituted following two statutory bodies under Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act to implement the Chapter IV ‘A’ of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act & Rules there-under: 
 i. A.S.U.D.T.A.B. (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Drug, Technical Advisory Board) 
 ii. A.S.U.D.C.C. (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Drug Consultative Committee) (under 
constitution) 
 The meeting of A.S.U.D.C.C. is to be convened every six months, wherein all State Drug 
Controllers will participate. In this committee, all aspects of quality control of A.S.U. drugs will be 
discussed and preventive/deterrent action will be initiated, whenever required, by the committee. 
 The above two statutory bodies are being activated. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is happy to note that two st atutory bodies under the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act, i.e. Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Drug, Technica l Advisory Board a nd Ayurveda, Siddha, 
Unani, Drug Consultative Committee have been  constituted by the Department. ASUDCC will 
be meeting every six months, with all the State Drug Controllers participating. This Committee 
will take care of all aspects of ASU (Ayurveda,  Siddha and Unani) drugs and will also initiate 
preventive/deterrent action whenever required. Th e Committee hopes that these two statutory 
bodies will be activated at the earliest. 
Recommendations/Observations 
16.6 The Committee understands that a Drug Control Cell (ISM) is working in the Department which 
besides other matters is also involved in the control of misbranded/adulterated and spurious 
manufacturing of AYUSH drugs. The Committee would like to be apprised about the work done by 
the Cell in this regard during the last two years. The Committee would also like to recommend that if 

need be, this Cell may be strengthened and function as a nodal agency in the vital area of curbing of 
manufacture and sale of spurious AYUSH drugs. 
Action Taken 
 The Drug quality control is the responsibility of the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) 
and the state licensing authorities. It is proposed to get the post of Additional Drug Controller 
(AYUSH) and Four Drug Inspectors (AYUSH) revived and filled to assist the DCGI in the task of 
quality control of AYUSH drugs. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is given to understand that dr ug quality control is the responsibility of the 
Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) and the state licensing authorities. The Committee 
would however like to point out that as per th e Annual Report of the Department for 2004-05 
Drug Control Cell in the Department is also in volved in the control of  misbranded/adulterated 
and spurious drugs of AYUSH, besides other ma tters. It seems that this Cell has not been 
handling the cases of misbranded/a dulterated and spurious drugs so  far. If not, the Committee 
would like to be apprised about the work done by the Cell during last two years. The Committee 
notes that the Department now proposes to get the post of Additional Drug Controller (AYUSH) 
and four Drugs Inspectors (AYUSH ) revived and filled up to assist  the DCGI in the task of 
quality control of AYUSH drugs. The Committee emphasizes that the Department should take 
all the required steps to implement the proposal at the earliest. 
Recommendations/Observations 
16.7 Committee’s attention has been drawn by some recent media coverage about a report published 
in the Journal of American Medica l Association. As per the report, a group of scientists of Harvard 
Medical School, Boston, USA picked up 70 Ayurvedic/Herbal Medicinal products manufactured by 
27 companies, 26 being Indian companies. The presen ce of metals in these products was more than 
permissible in food items in USA. The Committee has been informed that the Central Council for 
Research in Ayurveda and Siddha has already unde rtaken a study to see the safety profile of  
Ayurvedic drugs. Besides that, the Department has also approved a project to study the presence of 
various metals in normal habitat in raw drugs and classical Ayurvedic formulations. The Committee 
appreciates tile initiative taken by the Council and the Department. The Committee, however, feels 
that the Department should also inform the scientists of Harvard Medical School about the rationale 
for the presence of metals in Ayurvedic drugs and their safety aspect. 
Action Taken 
(i) The CCRAS has already undertaken a study to see the toxicity / safety profile of metal 
based bhasmas. The Study is being carried out in I.T.R.C., CSIR, Lucknow. The report of 
some drugs have been received, which are under examination by the experts in the 
Department. 
(ii) Department of AYUSH has also started a proj ect to estimate the presence of various metals 
in normal habitat in raw drugs and classical Ayurvedic formulations. The study is likely to 
be carried out in:- 
(a) Institute of Himalayan Bio-Resource Technology, CSIR, Palampur. 
(b) ITRC (Institute of Toxicolo gical Research Centre), CSIR  (Council for Scientific & 
Industrial Research), Lucknow. 
(c) IITC (Indian Institute of Toxicological Centre), Hyderabad. 
(d) A Delhi based laboratory. 

iii) The manufacturing companies, Ayurvedic medicines of which appeared in the news items 
have been asked to send safety profile of  their products including presence of heavy 
metals, etc. to the Department of AYUSH, at the earliest. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The report of scientists of USA mentioning the presence of metals in Ayurvedic/Herbal 
Medicinal products more than permissible limits is directly related to the efficacy and credibility 
of Ayurvedic medicines. The Committee appreciates  that the Department has initiated a study 
to see the toxicity/safety profile of metal base d bhasmas. A project to estimate the presence of 
various metals in normal habita t in raw drugs and classical Ay urvedic formulations has also 
been started. The Committee feels that findings of the study/project wo uld be available after 
some time only. However, it seems that Ha rvard Medical Associatio n has not been kept 
informed about the follow-up action taken by th e Department. If that be so, the Committee 
would impress upon the De partment to do so without any fu rther delay. Feedback from the 
manufacturing companies should also be expedited.

Comments of the Committee 
 Committee has observed that in spite of funds being provided for conducting elections to 
CCH year after year, elections could not be co nducted. The Committee is not satisfied with the 
justification for delay given by the Department. It seems that the process of notification for 
election and appointment of Returning officers is  a very cumbersome procedure as it has taken 
more than two years to complete this exercise. Wh at is more disturbing is that elections still 
remained to be conducte d, reason being non-ma intenance/updation of State Registers of 
Homoeopathy by the States. The Committee takes a serious view of this. The Committee fails to 
understand the lack of initiative on the part  of the CCH/Department in getting the State 
Registers updated well in time. The Committee is of  the view that the Department should take 
the required steps for streamlining the election procedure for CCH. (Para 3.4) 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been given to understand th at maintenance of Central Register of 
Indian Medicine and updati ng of the same is a continuous pr ocess. The Committee, however, is 
constrained to note that out of the eighteen States having State Boards, as on 31.03.05, Gujarat 
is the only State whose state Re gister is updated upto January, 2005 . In the case of rest of the 
States, pendency ranges from March 1983 in J&K to August 2004 in Delhi. Pendency in the 
State Registers has an adverse effect on the maintenance of Central Register. The Committee 
would therefore like to impress upon the Depart ment to vigorously pursue with the State 
Government the updation of the State Registers. 
 With regard to Central Register of Homoeo pathy, CCH is required to get renewed the 
registers after every eight years. The Committee fi n d s  t h a t  i n  r e s p e c t  o f majority of States, 
renewal has become due but it seems no action has been initiated so far. The Committee urges 
upon the Department to take the required action without any further delay. The Committee also 
observes that Central Register of Homoeopathy cannot be cons idered updated in any respect. It 
covers varying period from 1982 to 2004 in respect of different states. It seems Gazette 
Notifications are also being issued after al ong time-gap. Procedural formalities may be 
responsible for such a situation.  The Committee is of the firm op inion that entire procedure of 
maintenance and updation of both State and Central Regist ers for Indian Medicine and 
Homoeopathy needs to be reviewed so as to ensure its timely publication. (Para 3.5) 
Comments of the Committee 
 Committee had drawn the attention of the Department to there being no check on practice 
by non-qualified doctors and quacks. Reply of the Department, however, does not give any idea 
about the existence of any monitoring mechan ism either at State or Central level. The 
Committee would like to reiterate that there is an urgent need for taking an initiative by the 
Department in this area. Such a move would go a long way in curbing the unauthorized practice 
by AYUSH doctors and also increasing the faith of  general masses in the traditional system of 
medicine. (Para 3.6)

STATUS NOTE ON THE SCHEME FOR EXTRA MURAL RESEARCH IN AYUSH 
 The research in AYUSH sector was limited to the efforts made by the Central Research Councils, wh ich were largely in the natur e of clinical 
research and fell short of conforming to the modern scientific temper. Therefore, the Ministry felt the need for collaborative research arrangements with 
reputed research institutions and University Departments so as to generate a reliable and scientifically acceptable outcome. Ac cordingly, a Centrally 
Sector Scheme was launched in 1997-98. As the response to the Scheme was not very encouraging, the Scheme was revised in the ye ar 2001 by 
specifying the priority areas of research of the Department of AYUSH. Under the Scheme, funds are given to accredited research institutions, both 
Government and Non-Governmental Organizations, for undertaking time-bound research projects of one to three year durations. 
 Under the Scheme, a total of 67 projects have been sanctioned and total amount of Rs.7.26 crore has been utilized for undertak ing these projects so 
far. Year-wise break-up of funds utilization is given below:-

PREFACE 
 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to presen t the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Fortieth Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in the One Hundred Thirty 
Fourth Report on Demands for Grants 2022 -23 (Demand No. 46) of the Department of Health 
and Family Welfare (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare).  
2.  The 134th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 24th 
March, 2022.  The Department of Health and Family Welfare was forwarded the Action Taken 
Note on the recommendations/observations contained in the 1 34th Report within three months of 
the presentation of the Report in the Parliament. The Committee rece ived the Action Taken 
Notes on 26th July, 2022. 
3.  The Committee made a total of 77 recommendations in its 1 34th Report; out of which 25 
recommendations have been accepted by the Ministry and have been enumerated under Chapter 
I. Chapter II contains 14 recommendations, which the Committee does not desire to pursue in 
view of the Ministry‟s replies. In Chapter III there are 28 recommendations/observations in 
respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been accepted by the Committee and the 
Committee has made further recommendations thereon. While a total number of 10 
recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been 
received, has been categorized under Chapter IV. 
4.  The Committee, in its meeting held on t he 8th September, 2022 considered and adopted 
the draft Report.

1.1 Inter-State and intra-State disparity in healthcare infrastructure 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.1.1 The Committee is concerned at the existing wide inter -State and intra -State disparity 
in healthcare infrastructure across the country. Despite the much emphasized guidelines of 
the NHP, the States/UTs barring Delhi and Puducherry have not enhanced the shar e of 
health budget to more than 8% of the total State budget in the last 5 years. The Committee 
understands that States with poor financial resources and inefficient fiscal capacity have a 
herculean task ahead to overcome the situation of fragile health in frastructure vis-a-vis the 
demand of accessible and affordable healthcare facilities. The Committee is of the considered 
view that in order to maximise the benefits of economic, social and human capital, the States 
must invest in institutionalizing a robus t healthcare ecosystem that is capable of delivering 
adequate healthcare services to the masses on ground level especially in rural, urban and 
tribal region. The sooner the States realize the difference, a resilient and strong health system 
makes, the bett er will be the outcome on all social as well as economic indicators. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the States/UTs to emulate the UTs of Delhi and 
Puducherry and increase the share of health spending in their States Budget.  The Committee 
in this reg ard recommends the Department of Health and Family Welfare to persuade the 
State Governments to achieve the budgetary health expenditure to 8%. 
(Para 2.13 of 134th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2     The NHM expenditure, which is shared by both the Union and States will induce the 
State to further increase their budgetary allocation on health. As per the expenditure data of 
the union budget for 2018 -19 and 2019 -20 expenditure on NHM is more than 50 % clearly 
indicating the purpose of the union government. Apar t from the overall allocation, around 
20% of the allocation is kept under the NHM conditionality framework. This framework 
incentivizes the State to perform better on various health parameters and also penalizes the 
States for not meeting the targets. This  is a step toward s result-based financing and nudges 
the States towards improving their efficiency and the better performing States get more 
budgetary support. 
 
1.2 Health and Underperforming Sector  
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee noted that health has always remained an underperforming sector and 
despite funds allocation many States are not performing well on several health parameters. 
Many States lack the adequate absorption capacity to judiciously manage the allocated 
funds. The Committee, therefore,  recommends the Union Government to incentivise the 
States/UTs to make ground assessment of the efficacy of the health policies and help the 
States design policies suiting the needs of the respective region. The Union Government must 

2 
 
coordinate with the St ates to maximise the output under the Central Sector as well as 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  
(Para 2.14) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 The performance and the absorption capacities vary across the States. There are 
various reasons for this including capacities as well as governance issues which are beyond 
health sector. Under NHM, States are encouraged to take up assessment of efficacy of  
various health sector policies and schemes and dedicated budget lines are there to budget 
such activities. In order to focus on the outcomes, the MoHFW has decided an output 
matrix for the biennial PIPs. In discussion with the States, the level of achievement has been 
decided which would be monitored on a quarterly basis with the help of PMS and HMIS 
portal. 
1.3 Robust Health Policy and Judicious Allocation of Funds 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee is also of the opinion that robust health policies and judicious 
allocation of funds under different Schemes is fundamental for the optimal performance of 
the States/UTs. The Committee notes that healthcare services remain highly fragmented t hat 
further aggravates the problem of high OOPE in the country. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Ministry to make efforts in developing a better healthcare financing 
mechanism and ensuring the delivery of quality healthcare services.  
(Para 2.15) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 The Government is striving towards comprehensive care for all. In this direction, it 
has initiated the following programs which will have an impact on reducing Out of Pocket 
expenditure in the country and provide quality health care to the population: 
(i) Health and Wellness Centre under Ayushman Bharat is an attempt to move 
from a selective approach to health care to deliver a comprehensive range of 
services spanning preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative 
care. It has two components that are complementary to each other. Under its 
first component, 1,50,000 Health & Wellness Centres (HWCs) will be created 
to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care, that is universal and free to 
users, with a focus on wellness and  the delivery of an expanded range of 
services closer to the community.  
(ii) HWC is envisaged to deliver an expanded range of services that go beyond 
Maternal and child health care s ervices to include care for non - 
communicable diseases, palliative and r ehabilitative care, Oral, Eye, and ENT 
care, mental health and first -level care for emergencies and trauma, including 
free essential drugs and diagnostic services 
(iii) Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM -JAY): The second component is the 
Pradhan Mantri J an Arogya Yojana (PM -JAY) which provides health 

3 
 
insurance cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per year to over 10 crore poor and vulnerable 
families for seeking secondary and tertiary care. 
(iv) Free Drugs Initiatives: In 2015, under National Health Mission the 
government of India launched the Free Essential Drugs initiatives. Under this, 
free drugs are provided to all citizens in different levels of public health 
facilities.  
(v) Free Diagnostics Initiatives: The government of India under the National 
Health Mission (NHM ) launched the Free Essential Diagnostics in 2015. 
Under this initiative, a limited number of essential diagnostics at different 
levels of public health facilities are provided free to all citizens of India. 
(vi) Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Program: T his initiative was rolled out in 
2016 as part of NHM wherein quality dialysis services are provided „Free‟ to 
BPL patients and at nominal costs to others through Public -Private 
Partnerships. 
(vii) Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), wherein all servic es including, 
drugs, diagnostics, transport, diet, and blood transfusion (if necessary) are 
provided free to all pregnant women and children up to the age of one year.  
(viii) Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) wherein financial incentives are provided to 
mothers who underwent institutional deliveries. 
(ix) Free Treatment for TB under RNTCP: Under this scheme, free treatment 
services are available for TB at all Government hospitals, Community Health 
Centres (CHCs), and Primary Health Centres (PHCs). 
(x) Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK): RBSK was launched in 2013 as 
a new initiative aimed at screening over 27 Crore children from 0 to 18 years 
for 4 Ds -Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Development Delays 
including Disabilities. Children diagnosed  with illnesses receive follow up 
including surgeries at the tertiary level, free-of-cost. 
(xi) Ambulance Services under NHM: Launched in 2005 when the country didn‟t 
have an ambulance network.  At present, 31 States/UTs have a facility where 
people can dial 108 or 102 telephone numbers for calling an ambulance.108 is 
predominantly an emergency response system, primarily designed to attend to 
patients of critical care, trauma and accident victims, etc. 102 services 
essentially consist of basic patient trans port aimed to cater to the needs of 
pregnant women and children though other categories are also taking benefit 
and are not excluded. JSSK entitlements e.g., free transfer from home to 
facility, inter-facility transfers in case of referral and drop back fo r mother and 
children are the key focus of 102 services. 
(xii) Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan: Launched in 2016, this program 
aims to provide assured, comprehensive, and quality antenatal care, free of 
cost, universally to all pregnant women on the 9th of every month. The 
program aims to reach out to all Pregnant Women who are in the 2nd & 3rd 
Trimester of pregnancy.

2.2 Policy intervention to bridge infrastructure gaps 
Recommendation 
2.2.1 The Committee notes that in 2021-22, the country was engulfed by a deadly pandemic 
Covid-19 wave and the delivery of healthcare services was largely hampered. The pandemic 
brought forth in open the poor state of health infrastructure and necessitated Government's 
focus and Policy intervention to bridge infrastructure gaps to strengthen the healthcare 
facilities. It was anticipated that the ravages of t he pandemic will bring the attention of the 
Government to the rural -urban divide in the healthcare services and its delivery. However, 
just a 0.2 % increase in the BE of 2022 -23 in comparison to RE 2021 -22 reveals the 
reluctance of the Government in addres sing the immediate need of increasing public 
investments in the health sector. 
(Para 2.5) 
Action Taken 
2.2.2 It may be stated that in comparison to BE 2021 -22 of Rs. 71238.77 Crore,  the  RE 
2021-22 was enhanced due to  primarily one time Grant of Rs. 15728.22 Crore to combat 
CoVID-19 pandemic. With regard to 0.2 % increase in BE 2022 -23, Department of Health & 
Family Welfare have been allocated Rs. 83000.00 Crore in BE which is 16.50 % mo re than 

20 
 
the previous year (BE) Budgetary allocation. However, there has been a consistent effort in 
increasing the Budgetary outlay of the Department of Health and Family Welfare. 
2.2.3 In order to bridge infrastructure gaps to strengthen the health care f acilities in both 
rural-urban area in the country, Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Infrastructure Mission 
(PM-ABHIM) with an outlay of Rs. 64,180 crores over 5 years has been launched on 25th 
October-2021. In the current financial year, Rs. 5155.71 crore ha s been allocated for the said 
scheme. The scheme would develop capacities of primary, secondary, and tertiary care health 
systems, strengthen existing national institutions, and create new institutions, to cater to 
detection and cure of new and emerging diseases. 
2.3 Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS)  
Recommendations 
2.3.1 The Committee observes that the actual fund expenditure under the CGHS Scheme 
over the past few years has been higher than the allocation at BE stage. The Committee notes 
that a substantial part of the expenditure under the Budget is attributed to Pensions and 
Other Retirement Benefits (PORB). The Ministry must take special note of the budgetary 
expenditure and demands under the Scheme and ensure that adequate funds are allocated to 
the Scheme. The Committee is also of the view that all the CGHS beneficiaries should be 
provided with the cashless treatment facility at the empanelled hospitals and diagnostic 
centres.  The Committee has also come to know that many empanelled hospitals  avoid 
admitting CGHS beneficiaries stating that their bills are settled by the Ministry after a long 
time. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to prepare a time schedule for payment 
to the empanelled hospitals and ensure that there is no delay in p ayment to empanelled 
hospitals due to any shortage of funds under the budgetary head.  At the same time the 
Ministry must also ensure that the beneficiaries of CGHS get standard treatment at private 
hospitals and empanelled diagnostic centres. 
(Para 3.4) 
Action Taken 
2.3.2 Budget Estimates of CGHS are formulated based on the trend of expenditure in 
previous financial years. Payment of bills of empanelled private hospitals and diagnostic 
centres and also reimbursement to pensioner beneficiaries is made from Pension and other 
Retirement Benefits (PORB) Head. Shortfall, if any, is met from the enhanced allocation at 
RE stage. 
2.3.3 As per extant scheme guidelines, cashless treatment facility is provided only to certain 
specified categories of CGHS beneficiaries . Medical Reimbursement claims of serving 
central government employees are settled by the concerned Ministry/ Department from its 
own Budget Head. As the system of settlement medical reimbursement claims of serving 
employees is decentralized, it may not be  feasible to provide cashless facilities to the serving 
beneficiaries. 
2.3.4 Government has taken several measures to address the delay in settlement of the 
hospital bills as under, Bill processing has been shifted to NHA IT Platform for online 
settlement of hospital bills in a transparent and eco-friendly paperless mode.

3.3 Budgetary Allocation of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
Recommendation 
3.3.1 The Committee also notes that the budgetary allocation of Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare accounts f or 2.1% of the total BE 2022 -23 whereas the allocation for 
Ministry of Defence is 13.3% of the total budgeted expenditure of  the Government in 2022 -
23. The Committee realizes that for a country like India with limited State and Central 
Government funds, mobilization of resources poses a big cha llenge. However, this should not 
deter the Governments from increasing its health expenditure and according less priority to 
the health sector.   Health is one sector that can drive people to poverty and disrupt the 
economic conditions of families. Attenti on of the Committee has also been brought to the 
Tracking universal health coverage: 2017 Global Monitoring Report by WHO and World 
Bank that states, "Average 4.16 % of the population annually slips into poverty due to 
catastrophic health expenditure". The Committee reemphasizes that the importance of health 
sector must not be ignored and health must be given priority in terms of budgetary allocation. 
(Para 2.4) 
Action Taken 
3.3.2     India being a signatory to the SGD goals, achieving Universal Health coverage is one 
of the important targets. The National Health Policy also espouses similar sentiment as it has 
set a target of increasing government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP to e nsure affordable 
and accessible health services to all. Report by WHO and World Bank has identified that 
around 4.6% of the population falls below poverty line due to excessive health expenses. The 
recent NHA estimates for out –of – pocket expenditure (OOPE) on health (which might lead 
to financial vulnerability) and Government health expenditure do suggest that there has been 
a positive development in the country. The government health expenditure as a share of GDP 

31 
 
has increased from 1.15% in 2013 -14 to 1.35% in 2017-18. For the same period, the share of 
OOPE has declined from 64.2% to 48% 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.3     The Committee keeps into consideration the submission of the Secretary while 
giving his presentation to the Committee on DFG (2022 -23) th at as per the WHO's 
Global Health Expenditure Database 2018, the Government Health Expenditure as 
percentage of Current Health Expenditure is only 27% and the Out of Pocket 
Expenditure as percentage of the Current Health Expenditure is 62.7%. India ranks 
158 out of 196 countries in GHE as percentage of CHE and 176 out of 196 countries in 
OOPE as percentage of CHE . Expressing concern over the factual statement of the 
Secretary, Committee recommends the Department to approach Ministry of Finance to 
earmark budgetary allocation, at last 2.5% of GDP, as per target of National Health 
Policy to ensure affordable and accessible health services to all and also reduce the 
share of Out–of– Pocket Expenditure (OOPE).

3.5 Vacancy Position of CGHS 
Recommendations 
3.5.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that out of the sanctioned strength of 1531

3.13 National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP) 
Recommendation  
3.13.1 The Committee noted that the Ministry has not been able to utilize allocated  funds  
under the National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP). The Committee observes that organ 
donation rate in the country is very low when compared to other countries and there is a 
huge lack of awareness among the public. The Committee feels that India has a va st potential 
of organ donations and demand due to its population but the Ministry needs to make 
concerted efforts to develop such feelings amongst its citizens. NOTP aims to promote organ 
donation and transplantation across all States/Union Territories in the country. However, the 
Committee notes that performance of the program has been very poor which is reflected by 
huge underutilisation of funds under the Scheme. The Committee notes that the Scheme was 
allotted Rs. 30.50 crore in BE 2021 -22 which was sla shed to Rs. 6.39 crore in RE 2021 -22 
which is a 79% decrease with respect to BE 2021 -22. The Committee further notes that the 
program has been allotted a total of Rs. 15.00 crore in BE 2022-23.  
(Para 3.85) 
Action Taken 
3.13.2 One of the important objectiv es of National Organ Transplant Programme (NOTP) is 
to improve awareness about organ donation among the public. Towards this end the NOTTOs 
and SOTTOs have been conducting awareness activities on an ongoing basis right through 
the year. These awareness act ivities have led to increased pledging from the people. Most of 
these activities are pro bono activities at the level of the  
NOTTO/SOTTOs. Underutilization of IEC funds is mostly due to these being conducted on 
pro bono basis. 
3.13.3 NOTP is a central sect or continuing scheme. The scheme has been evaluated 
externally and found to be giving positive results in terms of increased awareness about organ 
donation, increase in number of deceased organ donations and establishments of organization 
for organ procure ment and distribution. The organ donation rate i.e. number of persons 
donating organs per million populations has increased from around 0.16 in 2012 to 0.52 in 
2019. Further, based on the feedback and past experience, to make the programme more 
effective and bridge the gap between demand for and supply of the organs for transplantation, 
some new components have been introduced in the programme such as support in facilitating 
medical education of doctors and staff of medical colleges/institutions (both Gover nment and 
Private) doing transplant activities or willing to start organ transplantation activities, training 
for transplant teams (surgeons, physicians, anaesthetists, nurses, technicians and perfusionists 
(in cases of heart and lung transplants) in India  or Abroad, setting up of 4 skills centres in 
NOTTO and medical colleges in the country, 10(ten) Regional/State Biomaterial Centres, 

42 
 
setting up of State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (SOTTOs) in each State, 
developing new/strengthening existing  retrieval and transplant centres, and support to 
retrieval centres. The SOTTOs are encouraged to send proposals to optimize utilization of 
funds for all the components of the programme. 
Further Recommendation  
3.13.4 The Committee appreciates that despite lower allocation of budget to NOTP and 
underutilization of IEC fund the organ donation rate has increased from 0.16 in 2012 to 
0.52 in 2019 due to enhanced impetus to organ donation awareness  campaign.  
However, the Committee observes that to make NOTP mo re effective and bridge the 
gap between demand and supply of the organs for transplantation , various new 
components have been incorporated in the programme viz. Medical Education for doing 
transplantation, training to transplants teams, setting up of 4 skills centers in NOTTO, 
10 Regional/State Bio-material centre, setting up of SOTTO in each State, strengthening 
existing retrieval and transplant centre etc.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to assess whether the continuing quantum of budge tary grant would be 
sufficient to meet the expenditure involving on various activities enshrined in new 
components of NOTP.

3.18.1 The Committee observes that the expenditure profile of all the initiatives under NHM 
has been satisfactory, however, there has been re-appropriation of funds from one pool to the 
other due to the pandemic Covid -19. The Committee notes that Ayushman Bharat Health-
Wellness Centres (AB -HWCs) is aimed at providing Comprehensive Primary Health Care 
(CPHC) to the masses. However, the Committee believes that along with increasing the 
number of these HWCs, the Ministry must also work towards enhancing the quality o f 
healthcare service delivery at these Centres. The Committee strongly recommends the 
Ministry to complete operationalization of the remaining HWCs and achieve the target of 
setting up of 1,50,000 functional HWCs by December 2022. The Ministry must also wo rk 
towards augmenting the Health care facilities by including tele -medicine, Yoga and mental 
health care services in these HWCs.  
(Para 4.19) 
Action Taken  
 
3.18.2 The National Health Policy 2017 envisages the goal of attainment of the highest 
possible lev el of health and well -being, through a preventive and promotive health care 
orientation, and universal access to good quality health care services without anyone having 
to face financial hardships as a consequence. To progressively achieve Universal Health  
Coverage, Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) was 
launched in 2018 to deliver Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services. With a target of 

46 
 
1,50,000 Health and Wellness Centres by December, 2022, the existing Sub -Health Centres 
(SHC), Primary Health Centres (PHC) and Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHC) are being 
transformed into AB -HWCs to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) that 
includes preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and rehabilitative services which is 
universal, free, and close to the community. As on 30th June, 2022, total 1,20,112 AB -HWCs 
which includes 92,470 SHCs, 22,915 PHCs and 4,727 UPHCs, have been operationalized 
throughout the country against the operationalization target of 1,50,000 AB -HWCs by 
December, 2022. 
 
3.18.3 The measures undertaken for the approved centres to be recognized as functional AB -
HWC are: 
 
1) HR - availability - To improve the delivery mechanism, a new cadre of healthcare 
providers are introduced at the mid -level with educational back grounds such as 
B.Sc in Community Health or a Nurse (GNM or B.SC) or an Ayurveda 
Practitioners with due certification in public health. These Mid -Level HealthCare 
Providers are designated as Community Health Officer (CHO). The CHO at SHC -
HWC carry out publ ic health functions, ambulatory care, and management and 
provide leadership at the Sub-Health Centre-Health and Wellness Centres. 
 
2) Infrastructure - All AB -HWCs are provided with sufficient space for outpatient 
care, for dispensing medicines, diagnostic services, adequate spaces for display of 
communication material of health messages, including audio visual aids and 
appropriate community spaces for wellness activities, including the practice of 
Yoga and physical exercises. 
 
3) Availability of Free Medicines  - Number of essential medicines at PHC -HWCs 
have been increased to 172 and at the SHC -HWCs, these have been increased to 
105. The CHO at the SHC -HWCs dispense medicines based on treatment plans 
initiated by the medical officer at the PHC-HWC. 
 
4) Availability of Free Diagnostics -Number of essential diagnostic tests have been 
increased to 63 in PHC -HWCs and 14 in SHC -HWC. Completion of CBAC 
enumeration for NCDs and CDs - Community-Based Assessment Check list is 
administered by the ASHA for each individual abo ve 30 years at the household 
level. This captures the risk for various illness and also enables screening by MPW 
and referral to the nearest Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centre (AB -
HWC). 
 
6)    Capacity building of primary healthcare team on expanded  package of services - 
The MO, ASHAs and ANMs have been trained in the 7 basic services. The  
Community Health Officer undergone 15 days Expanded Induction training after 
their posting at SHC -HWC. This training covers sessions on RMNCHA+N, 
Communicable diseases, non-communicable diseases, and Jan Aarogyasamiti. 
 
7) Expanded Service Delivery- The existing package of Primary Health Care services 
is being expanded to go beyond Reproductive and Child Health and 
Communicable Diseases to include comprehensive primary health care services for 
non-communicable diseases, Mental Health, ENT, Ophthalmology, Oralhealth, 
Geriatric and Palliative healthcare and first level care for emergencies and traumas 

47 
 
well as Health promotion and wellness activities like Yoga. About 1.18 Cr 
Wellness Sessions, including Yoga, has been conducted at AB -HWCs & 60.46 Cr 
Screenings for NCDs (Hypertension/ Diabetes/ Oral, breast & cervical cancer) has 
been done as on 10.06.2022. 
 
8)    Robust IT system- AB-HWC portal and app has been developed and being used by 
the States/UTs to capture progress on AB -HWC operationalization. Tablets are 
being provided at AB -HWC for operationalization and digitization of the health 
information. Total Teleconsultation sundere-Sanjeevani is 3.90 crores (as on 
30.06.2022). E-Sanjeevani HWC is operational at 94,599 Spokes & 10,709 Hubs 
(including Spoke cum hubs). 
 
9) Financing/provider payment reforms -Performance linked payment is being 
provided to CHOs and primary healthcare team at HWC. 
 
10)    Community mobilisation and health promotion through activities like Fit Health 
Worker Campaign, Eat Right India movement, Annual health calendar for 
promoting wellness related activities. 
 
3.18.4 Additionally, to ensure an in tegrated approach of primary healthcare, various 
community platforms, namely Jan Arogya Samiti (JAS), Village Health, Sanitation and 
Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) and Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS) are being created and 
engaged the level of community and AB-HWCs. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.18.5 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in operationalizing 
a total of 1,20,112 AB-HWCs throughout the country against the target of 1,50, 000 AB-
HWCs by December, 2022. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry 
will make all out effort to achieve the target of op erationalizing 1,50,000 AB -HWCs in 
order to provide Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services across the country.  T he 
Committee further recommends that all these centre must have adequate human 
resource with 4 technical expertise and latest tools and techniques, diagnostic kits, 
medicines to provide quality healthcare service and standard treatment.  The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry should popularize tele -consultation Sundere-
Sanjeevani in rural areas.

Recommendation

provide greater flexibility to States/UTs for appropriation of funds. However, the Committee

recommends the Ministry to coordinate with the States/UTs for timely submission of

poor track record on health indicators and monitor their progress under each component of

proposals from States for Strengthening of State Drug Regulatory System has been one of the

persuaded to submit the project proposals matching to the indicative amount. The Ministry

may also follow up with all the States and make efforts to set up sufficient number of 
laboratories The Committee empha sizes on the need of cooperation between the States and

strengthening the drug regulatory environment in the country.
