3. Thereafter, the Chairman welcomed the witnesses and  asked them to apprise the Committee 
about the severity of TB burden on the country, the causes behind high incidence of TB cases in our 
country, the challenges faced by TB p atients, availability of accessible and affordable diagnostic and 
treatment facilities, the impact of Covid -19 on healthcare facilities for TB patients, and the role of 
alternative system of medicines in management of TB. The Chairman further asked the witnesses to 
apprise the Committee about their views on progress made so far in TB elimination, further measures 
required to meet the goal of ending TB by 2025 and future 'course of action' to achieve the targets. 
4. Prof (Dr.) Ravindra Kumar Dewan  then made a p resentation on the subject and inter-alia 
highlighted the following key points:  
(i) The Government of India first adopted the National TB Programme in 1962, which was based 
on mass miniature radiography, that is, going to the field, doing  x -rays and finding the 
patients who were positive; 
(ii) In 1997, the Revised National TB Control Programme was adopted in which the diagnostic 
was based on sputum examination followed by six months treatment which was directly 
observed; 
(iii) As per the definition adopted by Sustainabl e Development Goals, “ending TB means 
reduction by 80 per cent of the incidence”; 
(iv) On an average, at most of the places where the patient deposits their sputum there is lag time 
of 15-20 days before the diagnosis is made; 
(v) The majority of the patients of TB are still being treated in the private sector and the 
Government sector  treats 25 to 30 per cent only, also in private hospitals the notification of 
TB cases in not accurate;  
(vi) Many complications during and after the treatment require surgical intervention s like thoracic 
surgeries, however, there  are only five or six centres who can do thoracic surgery for TB 
patients in the country; 
(vii) Many a times TB patients require trained counsellors who can impress upon them the need to 
complete treatment, help in manag ing adverse effects of drugs and counselling regarding 
other aspects of health and hygiene; 
(viii) India's programme to tackle TB is the best amongst all the South Asian countries; 
(ix) As per the latest report of 2022, the States like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtr a, Assam and 
Madhya Pradesh are the biggest hotspots of TB; 
(x) India continues to have the largest burden of TB patients i.e. 24 per cent of the global TB 
incidence. 
(xi) The reasons for high incidence of TB in India specially are huge and dense population, 
migrant population in search of employment, poor nutrition, socio -economic status of large 
segments of our population, unhygienic practices like spitting in public places and not 
following the respiratory and cough hygiene;  
(xii) Another major reason for high inciden ce of TB in India is high incidence of anaemia 
primarily in children and young population; low vitamin -D levels, lack of exposure to 
sunshine as well as lack of milk products in the diet affects the response to the treatment 
provided; 

85 
 
(xiii) Patients addicted to smoking, alcohol and drugs are more susceptible to develop TB. Also, 
they do not show adequate response to treatment;   
(xiv) “Nikshay” software which is used by doctors for notification of TB cases is slightly not user 
friendly and should be revamped for improving its use; 
(xv) “Incomplete treatment” is a major concern mainly because of two reasons, after three to four 
weeks of treatment patients start feeling well and stop the treatment, another reason is 
migrant population; 
(xvi) Early diagnosis and availability and acce ssibility of TB treatment has to be ensured and 
should be uninterrupted; 
(xvii) To deal with the stigma associated with TB, Central TB Division has adopted the concept 
called 'TB Champions' wherein those people who have tackled TB and become completely 
cured, highlight these issues in community at various levels;  
(xviii) Health, hygiene and issues related to this respiratory hygiene need to be an integral part of 
school and college curriculum as that is an impressionable age and thus this age group can be 
sensitized towards importance of health and cleanliness; and 
(xix) Recently, TB preventive treatment programme has been introduced, under which the 
household contacts of the diagnosed or positive patients are given the TB preventive 
treatment.   
5. Thereafter, Dr. K. K. Chopra, in his presentation, inter alia highlighted the following points:- 
(i) “End TB by 2025” is targeted to reduce TB deaths from 36 per lakh population to 3 per lakh 
population by 2025; 
(ii) At present the TB notification is 172 per lakh population per year, out of which 120 per lakh 
per year is from public sector and 52 per lakh per year is from the private sector;  
(iii) In 2022, the Presumptive TB Examination Rate (PTBER) for the country rose to 1281 per 
lakh population (68% increase) from 763 in 2021; 
(iv) Around 14 lakh patients have been put on TB preventive treatment so as to avoid emergence 
of disease among contacts of TB cases; 
(v) Under Nikshay Poshan Yojana, Rs.500 is given to every patient till the treatment continues; 
(vi) At national level the t reatment success rate in the country is around 86 per cent and death 
rate is around 2 to 3 percent. The remaining patients either defaults or leaves;   
(vii) Rapid urbanisation has caused the problem to aggravate, as 30% of country’s population is 
migratory; 
(viii) In India, the most common cause  of TB is under -nutrition, after which alcohol  drug abuse, 
smoking, diabetes and HIV are major drivers;  
(ix) Newer drugs used for treatment of TB are restricted to public sector, private sector has no 
access to them, but since lar ge percent of TB patients report to the private sector there is 
need to ease the accessibility of such drugs;  
(x) More than 80% of  patients are getting the community support by CSR or individual 
support; 
(xi) Out of the 13,90,840 TB patients undergoing treatment currently, around ten lakh patients 
are getting support with the help of around 80,000 Ni -Kshay Mitra registered under the 
programme; and 
(xii) At present, the notification of TB patients from the private sector is about 40 per cent at the 
national level. 
6. Lastly, Dr. Salil Bhargava and Cmde Raman Arora (retd.)  made a presentation which inter 
alia highlighted the following points:- 

86 
 
(i) Implementation of e -PDSA (Electronic Plan Do Study Act) in districts is improving TB 
notification; 
(ii) The role of District TB officers and the need to build their capacity in the areas of 
leadership and quality improvement is pivotal for TB management in the country;   
(iii) There is need of awareness programs in respect of improvement in etiquettes and behavior  
of people in public place like spitting, chewing pan, gutkha, etc; 
(iv) National TB Prevalence Survey shows that out of 100 TB cases, symptoms based diagnosis 
picks up only 62 cases while x-ray based diagnosis picks up 95 cases which depict that more 
x-ray machines are needed; 
(v) Among one lakh TB patients, microscopy picks up 152 TB patients while molecular tests 
(like CBNAAT) picks up 285. Hence the program must pivot from microscopy diagnosis to 
molecular diagnosis; 
(vi) As per Prevalence Survey, active case findings get about 318 cases per lakh while passive 
reporting by notification is around 218 per lakh. Hospital inpatients need to be screened for 
TB;  
(vii) Symptoms of TB like fever, cough, weight -loss are ignored by 70% of  patients. Ignoring 
symptoms leads to ongoing transmission and delay in diagnosis . Every touch point in health 
care need to ask 5 symptom questions; and  
(viii) Risk of TB is highest in first two years after exposure and then declines. In view thereof, 
persons in contact of TB patients like family members, workplace colleagues, etc. must get 
TB prevention therapy to curb the transmission of the disease.

2.3
             The Committee observes that in accordance with the goals as contained in the NHP-2002, allocation for central
health sector should imply a manifold increase in the budget requirement. The Committee is in agreement with the
contention of the Department that past trends of allocation of budgetary outlays and the overall resources constraint do
not indicate a very encouraging scenario. Two suggestions were put forth before the committee in this regards by the
Department. First was that the external assistance for different schemes being obtained from various agencies as grants
be taken as an additionally over and above the budget. Committee was given to understand that a major constraint of
National AIDS Control Programme has been that of external assistance which comes from through Gross Budgetary
Support as a result of which all external assistance has to be accommodated within the Annual Plan/Five Year Plan
outlay ceiling. The Committee is in agreement with the viewpoint of the Department that external assistance coming in
the shape of grant-in-aid (distinct from loan) should flow over and above the Gross Budgetary Support, The Committee,
accordingly recommends that the Department should take up this issue with the Planning Commission.

measures in some states are not proving effective as the number of Malaria deaths instead of showing any downward
trend seem to be increasing. The committee is of the view that Department should take the initiative in coordination with
the concerned state Govts, who are implementing agencies for monitoring Malaria Control Programme in those States
showing increasing number of cases and deaths during the recent years.

Action Taken
           Maximum no. of deaths are reported from the states of Assam, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Mizoram,
Orissa, Rajasthan and West Bengal which contribute about 90% of the total deaths in the country.  The no. of deaths
have decreased in almost all the states since 2001 except marginal increase in the states of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh,
Mizoram and Punjab. Major increase has been reported from Gujarat, Maharashtra, Manipur, Rajasthan, Tripura and
West Bengal where substantial no. of deaths have been reported.Overall, no. of malaria cases in the country has
decreased by about 10.36% in 2003 as compared to 2001. However cases have shown slight increasing trend in the states
of Gujarat, Haryana, Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh, Daman
& Diu and Lakshadweep in 2003 as compared to 2001.
The state authorities have been advised to strengthen the surveillance activities to control the morbidity and
mortality due to malaria. Besides, Govt. of India is sending teams to the states from this organization and other
institutions like ICMR to provide the technical assistance to the states to plan and implement the programme effectively.
 
10.6 Recommendations/Observations
The committee finds that the situation in Bihar is more alarming. Most of the Districts in the state had ABER of
less than 1% in the Year 2003, due to which actual magnitude of Malaria situation in the State could not be assessed.
There are some districts like Aurangabad, Bhagalpur, Gaya, Patna, Nawada etc, where even with low level of ABER,
high Plasmodium Falciparum (Pf) proportion are being reported. The Committee would like to point out that the
Department should make all possible efforts for activating the existing/required machinery for the proper implementation
of the programme. The Committee strongly feels that the Department will have to continue monitoring by sending
inspection teams to the affected districts of the state.

11.5 Recommendations/Observations
The Committee notes with serious concern the WHO estimates of approximately 18 lakh new cases reported in
the country every year, out of which 8 lakh are new smear positive highly infectious cases. The Committee notes that
massive funding andtrained manpower along with a very large number of NGOs and private practitioners failed to keep
pace with the reported expansions of disease. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that there seems to be a need for
refocussing on vulnerable areas. It seems that the ground realities do not seem to be very conducive in all the states.
Therefore, district specific implementation of the programme is the need of the hour. For example, one practical problem
being observed is that drugs are being prescribed for very short period and for that too patients have to cover a very long
distance from their home to the clinic. Not only this, there are areas where hospitals are not ideally located. The
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that some element of flexibility should be permissible in the implementation of the
Programme. The Committee also feels that it should be ensured that there is more active participation both from
NGOs/Private practitioners on vulnerable areas, even if they are not conveniently located.
 
Action Taken
The RNTCP is an application of WHO recommended strategy of Directly Observed Treatment Short Course
(DOTS). Under this strategy to ensure compliance to treatment, the intensive phase of treatment, drugs are administered
thrice a week to the TB patient under the direct observation. This is only for first 2-3 months of the treatment. In the
continuation phase of treatment out of three doses in  week, first dose is given under observation and the remaining two
doses are self administered by the patient. The period of continuation phase is 4-5 months.For the convenience of the TB
patients, DOTS centres are established near to their residences. Any person such as voluntary health worker, anganwadi
worker, panchayat raj functionary, women self help group, who is accountable to health system and acceptable to the TB
patient can function as a DOT provider. The premises of the DOT providers are designated as DOT centres. Thus the
programme is providing necessary flexibilities to the districts as  DOT Centres can be established at convenient distance.
Anti TB drugs are provided in patient-wise boxes to ensure that all drugs required for full course of treatment are
earmarked the day one a TB patient is registered for treatment. The program is implemented by the District TB Societies
and they have flexibility in establishing the microscopy centres to be area specific. To increase the accessibility of the
masses to the TB care facilities, special emphasis is laid on involvement of NGOs and Private Practitioners which has
been decentralized to the district level. Presently, more than 1000 NGOs and more than 5000 Private Practitioners are
working for the TB Programme.

XX. RABBIES CONTROL
 
20.2
         Recommendations/Observations
The Committee has observed that India is the only country in the world using Nerve Tissue Rabies Vaccine
(NTV), where under 14 ver painful injections are given in the abdomen of patients.   This vaccine is being manufacture
and used in our counrty til date whereas other countries including Pakistan and Bangladesh have abandoned the same ten
years ago.  The World Health Organisation (WHO) three decades ago recommended a worldwide ban on the use of NTV
and switch over to the tissues culture anti rabies vaccine (TCVs).  The Committee notes that the Health Planning
Committee has also recommended the switching over to Tissue Culture Vaccine (TCVs).  Under TCV six injections are
given in the arm which are not only safe and painless but cost effective also.  The Committee understands that these
vaccines are being manufactured by several private and public sector institutes like Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (owned
by the National Dairy Development Board) and Human Biologicals Institute are producing the Tissue Culture Vaccines
(TCVs) – which is not made from live cells but from dead cells which are cloned in test tubes in a healthy and efficient
manner.  Aventis Pharma Ltd. produces the excellent Rabipur.  All of them are available for approximately the same cost
as the NTV.  The committee also finds that whereas NTV has shelf life of 6 months, the TCV has a shelf life of 24
months.  The Committee recommends that the Department should initiate action for introduction of TCVs for use all
over the country. 
 
Action Taken
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has already decided to phase out the production of NTV and switch over to
the use of Tissue Culture Anti Rabies Vaccine (TCARV) with effect from 01
st January 2005.  The production of NTV in
the country has been completely stopped and the manufacturing units have been allowed to sell NTV beyond 1 st January
2005 only till the stock is completely exhausted.  All the State Governments have been requested to switch over to the
use of TCARV for post exposure treatment of animal bites cases.

XIII. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME
13.1         Recommendations/Observations
India has an estimated number of 5.1 million HIV infected persons by 2003. The spread of HIV infection is not
uniform across the states in the country.  Six states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Nagaland, Manipur, Maharashtra and
Tamil Nadu are categorised as high prevalence states. Gujarat, Pondicherry and Goa are categorised as states with
moderate prevalence of HIV. All the remaining States/U.Ts are categorised as low prevalence States.
A comprehensive National AIDS control Programme Phase II is currently under implementation throughout the
country as a centrally sponsored scheme. The programme has five components as indicated below:
 
*         Priority targeted interventions for population at high risk.
*         Preventive interventions for the general population.
*         Low cost care for people living with HIV/AIDS.
*         Institutional strengthening.
*         Inter-Sectoral Collaboration.
 
Action Taken
National AIDS Control Organisation conducts annual round of HIV Sentinel Surveillance to monitor HIV trends
in various risk groups of population. This data is also used to estimate number of HIV infection in the country. Based on
2004 round of HIV Sentinel Surveillance conducted in 659 Sentinel Sites in the country, it is estimated that there are
5.134 million infections in the country. It is also observed that the spread of HIV infection is not uniform across the
states in the country. However, the stage of the epidemic in a particular state remains unchanged as compared to
previous years.
It is true that a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme Phase II is currently under implementation
throughout the country as a centrally sponsored scheme. This phase will be under implementation till March 2006.
Preparation for phase III of the programme has also been started.
 
13.4
         Recommendations/Observations
While appreciating the inbuilt monitoring mechanism under the programme, the committee would like to have
the details of financial assistance released to NGOs during 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05. The committee would also
like to have the details of NGOs found to be indulging in malpractices during this period, state wise and action taken
against them. The committee observes that the level of involvement of NGOs in the programme seems to depend upon
the number of active NGOs coming forward in a particular area. The committee feels that if this is the position, then
there is a need for reviewing the criteria for selection of NGOs. Number of NGOs should be regulated by the existing
HIV risk population. There should be a specific norm for restricting the number of NGOs in a particular area.
 
Action Taken

being implemented by 58 NGOs across the country. It is ensured that NGO located at one project area   does not get

links with the community.  In order to ensure that these interventions are cost effective and comprehensive, NACO has
provided guidelines for assessing the costs of proposed interventions for specific groups. The guidelines assist SACS to
sanction projects whose budgetary and programmatic scope is authentic and appropriate. The administrative approval for

13.11    Recommendations/Observations
The most important recommendation of the Working Group was agreement reached with pharmaceutical
companies on the prices of fixed dose combinations of ART drugs.  These prices were to be applicable only to the
quantity procured by Govt.  In the open market, the market forces were to determine the prices of the anti-retroviral
drugs.  The rates offered by the pharmaceutical companies to Govt. were subject to 100% waiver on excise duty, Central
Sales tax on major ingredients of raw materials and 100% custom duty waiver on imported material.
 
Action Taken
NACO is perusing with the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers for the  exemption/reduction of custom duty on
raw material and intermediates which are imported and  used for manufacturing ARV drugs by indigenous
pharmaceutical companies. However, as most of these raw material/intermediates are used for purposes other than
manufacturing ARV drugs, it has to be ensured that such exemptions are not misused. Therefore, pharmaceutical
companies are required to submit the precise proportion ingredient raw material/intermediate used for manufacturing
ARV drugs. However, NACO has already been able to purchase the ARV drugs in the year 2004-05 at rates much lower
than the rates indicated by the pharmaceutical companies at the time of above-mentioned Working Group meeting.
To sum up following measures have brought about the reduction in the cost of ARV drugs used in Govt
Hospitals:
i)                             Exemption from payment of central excise duty on the generic ARV drugs and their formulations used for
treatment of AIDS cases. Currently, the ARV drugs exempted from the payment of central excise duty include
Stavudine, Zidovudine, Didanosine, Nevirapine, Efavirenz, Nelfinavir, Indinavir, Ritonavir, Saquinavir and Lamivudine.
ii) Exemption from the payment of custom duty and counterveiling duty on import of bulk generic ARV drugs, such as,
Ritonavir and Saquinavir and their formulations.

13.12 Recommendations/Observations
The Report of the Working Group indicates that approximately 100,000 AIDS cases were sought to be covered
during the first year of the treatment and thereafter a 10-15% increase in the number of AIDS cases was anticipated.  The
Committee would like to be apprised about the strategy adopted for procurement of anti-retroviral drugs provided free of
cost on a pilot project basis in 2004 to a selected small number of patients.  The Committee would also like to know
about the fate of the report of the Working Group given in 2003.
 
Action Taken
Free Anti Retroviral Therapy (ART) was initially started in eight ART Centres, established in tertiary level
medical institutions/hospitals in six High Prevalence States and NCT Delhi. This was scaled up to 25 ART Centres in 13
States / UTs by 31st March 2005. It has been planned that by end current Financial Year, free ART will be provided from
a total of 100 hospitals
A total of 9168 patients are reported to be receiving ART from 25 ART Centres till 31st   May 2005.
For procurement of ARV drugs provided free of cost, NACO has adopted the strategy of using only the generic
ARV drugs manufactured by indigenous pharmaceuticals using ARV drugs approved by Drug Controller General of
India (DCGI) and not restricting to the list of WHO pre qualified ARV drugs.   Quality assurance for DCGI approved
ARV drugs is by conducting tests in high quality laboratories in India.
For this, open competitive tender process inviting tenders from all eligible suppliers through wide publicity is
followed.
This has reduced the average prices to as low as Rs 5500 per person per year compared to the average cost of Rs
16,000 per person per year one year ago. At present the low end ARV combination drugs are available at Rs 3,500 per
person per year and high end drugs used for certain categories, such as HIV with TB patients, at Rs 6,500 per person per
year as against the costs of Rs 14,400 and Rs 18,000 per person per year respectively one year ago.

II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.4   Recommendations/Observations
The Department has also advocated that on the analogy of 2% Education Cess, a similar cess may also be
introduced in the health sector to enable realization of the goal of raising public spending on health to at least 2% of
GDP over the next five years. The Committee, however, has serious reservations on this proposal, not only due to such a
cess involving taxpayer’s money but also due to the past record of utilization of funds by the department. While not
denying that approved outlay for 2005-06 will adversely affect a number of schemes, the most affected being the
ambitious ‘Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Srakshana Yojana’ the Committee is more perturbed by the trend of allocation on
non-plan funds. Non-provision of required non-plan funds for the premier hospitals like AIIMS, PGIMER Chandigarh,
NIMHANS, Bangalore, even affecting the salary component of the staff is a matter of serious concern.
 
Action Taken
Under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana(PMSSY), Rs. 250 crores has been approved in the Annual
Plan 2005-06.  This lower order of funding against the proposed outlay was agreed to as the scheme was still under
formulation and the necessary approvals awaited.
 The Ministry has been approaching the Ministry of Finance to provide non-plan funds for premier hospitals like
AIIMS, PGIMER Chandigarh, NIMHANS Bangalore and similarly placed many other prestigious institutes. But from
past few years the Ministry of Finance has not been able to meet the requisite Non-Plan allocation to the Health Sector.
 
2.6 Recommendations/Observations
              The Committee is dismayed to note that as a result of declining trend of allocation of non-plan funds,
department is compelled to divert plan funds to non-plan to meet the obligations of some major health institutions. The
Committee feels that this can not be considered a healthy development, being against the prescribed norms. Diversion of
Plan funds to non-plan side very well indicated the poor status of schemes of the department, very vital for the
development of the country as a whole. While on one side, Department is advocating impositions of 2% cess for
generation of additional funds, it is not in a position to utilize the allocated plan funds due to poor management and
incapacity of implementing agencies. The Committee would like to emphasize that the Department should take remedial
measure in the light of finding of mid-term appraisal of various schemes.
 
Action Taken
We agree with recommendation of the committee that diversion of funds from plan to non-plan is not a healthy
trend. However, this apparently had been resorted to by the Ministry on account of shortage of funds under the non-plan
in respect of certain major health institutions like AIIMS, NIMHANS, VPCI etc.  The Ministry of Finance has been
approached even at the level of the Minister of Health to provide adequate Non-Plan budget to avoid diversion from Plan
to Non-Plan.
 
Comments of the Committee

3.10 Recommendations/Observations
The Committee is unhappy to note that the CGHS network has not been able to achieve its desired objective of
providing efficient medical service to its beneficiaries. The network of CGHS dispensaries has degenerated to a stage
where patients receive neither treatment nor consultation. In fact, beneficiaries with very basis ailments only such as cold
and cough are attended to in these dispensaries. In Committee’s view, the position today is that treatment of the
beneficiaries is practically taking place at the specialist level only in a few hospitals and in designated dispensaries in
Delhi, and the number of specialists available in Delhi vis-à-vis CGHS beneficiaries is very low. Position of CGHS
beneficiaries residing in NCR such as Noida, Gurgaon is more worse as they are given dates of visit by specialists,
sometimes ranging from 45 days to 60 days and the beneficiaries have to wait for the arrival of specialists for long
periods. Therefore, the idea of providing a convenient health care to the Central Government employees has remained a
dream. The Committee strongly recommends that Government should take immediate steps to ensure that CGHS
dispensaries function in such a manner that the dispensaries, instead of being a place for referring patients to specialists
and disbursement of medicines recommended by them, should become health centers where its beneficiaries actually
receive proper treatment. It is high time that the role and functions of CGHS dispensaries
 is re-determined.

8.4
  Recommendations/Observations
Committee’s attention has also been drawn by media reports about several clinics promising Stem cell cure for
diseases from Muscular Dystrophy, Neuromucsular disorder, Stroke, Liver Cirrhosis, Diabetes etc. in Delhi and other
cities in the country. When asked about the authenticity of such claims, the Director General, ICMR informed the

the source of stem cell used for therapy. The applicant, however, failed to provide the same even after several reminders.
 
Action Taken
The beneficial effects of Stem Cell research as therapy have been acknowledged by all the scientific departments
in the country who have announced that this should be promoted and supported in the country with adequate
regulatory/monitoring mechanism in view of the ethical, legal and social issues involved. The draft guidelines in this
regard were prepared earlier. A brainstorming session is being planned by the ICMR  to come out with a National Policy
and appropriate guidelines for Stem Cell research and clinical application in the country.
 
8.5  Recommendations/Observations
As informed by ICMR, in view of the potential of this new technology in modern therapeutics and biomedical
research, a brain storming session was organised at the Institute of Pathology, New Delhi on 14 th September, 2001.  It
was decided that Stem Cell research and its clinical applications should be promoted in the country.  However, need for
thorough examination of this new technology before approving any research was also emphasised.  Accordingly, DCGI
requested ICMR to prepare appropriate guidelines to help in regulation of Stem Cell research and its research and its
application.  A drafting Committee was constituted for this purpose which drafted  brief guidelines on the subject in
2002.  These draft guidelines were put on ICMR Website for public consultation and also sent to DCGI for approval. 
The Committee has been given to understand that comments and suggestions have been received and the document is
being finalised.
 
8.6. Recommendations/Observations
The Committee notes that the guidelines suggest that a multi-disciplinary National Apex Committee  should be
constituted to monitor Stem Cell research activities in the country.  All proposals involving stem cells of an source will
be examined by this Committee.   Centres involved in Stem Cell research will have to be registered with the Committee. 
While appreciating the initiative taken by the Council for regulation of Stem Cell research and its application, the
Committee would like to emphasise that the approval process of draft guidelines on the subject pending before DCGI
should be expedited.  This is very necessary in view of a number of clinics claiming successful results in the treatment of
hitherto incurable diseases have started operation in recent years.  The Committee would also appreciate if an initiative is
taken by the ICMR/Department/concerned authorities in taking preventive steps so that such clinics do not continue to
attract patients.
 
Comments of the Committee
           Media report continue to come about significant achievements being made in Stem Cell Therapy.  The Committee
has commented extensively in this regard in its Seventh Report presented to Parliament in April, 2005. The Committee
was given to understand that draft guidelines for helping in regulation of Stem Cell research had been put on the ICMR
Website.  These guidelines suggested constitution of a multi-disciplinary National Apex Committee. The Committee had
suggested that the approval process of draft guidelines pending before DCGI should be expedited.  Latest Report
furnished by the Department however, indicates that the draft guidelines for which a drafting Committee was set up in
2002 continue to remain at the draft stage even after a gap of three years.  What is even more surprising is that a
brainstorming Session is now being planned by ICMR to come out with a National Policy and appropriate guidelines for
Stem Cell research.  The Committee is not happy with this kind of approach.  More than three years have passed since
the constitution of Drafting Committee in November, 2002.   The Committee strongly feels that there is a need both for
extensive research in Stem Cell therapy promising cure of chronic health problems and also regulating false claims in
this area.

13.14 Recommendations/Observations
“The Committee also notes a very disturbing observation made in the Audit Report. It has been pointed out that
although the Ministry had announced in December 2002 that blood donors found to be HIV positive would be told of
their infection and asked to seek confirmatory tests and counseling, NACO continues to follow the existing policy of
giving the results only to those persons who ask for these. The Committee agrees with the audit observation that non-
disclosure of HIV status; mandatory to all HIV infected reasons could lead to such persons unknowingly spreading the
disease among the uninfected persons. The Committee is not inclined to accept the argument of the Department that HIV
status is revealed only to those donors who would want their status known, as any other approach will adversely affect
voluntary blood donation movement. The Committee would like to emphasize that a rethinking is required on this
sensitive issue in view of the dangerous implications of this policy.”
 
Action Taken
Presently the policy envisages the reveal of HIV status only to result seeking donors.  This can be debated by a
group of experts, to build up consensus to include all donors instead of restricting only to result seeking donors. 
Subsequently, National AIDS Control Board (NACB) approval will be required.
 
Comments of the Committee
In its earlier report, the Committee had drawn the attention of the Department to an observation made in the CAG
Report of 2004 about the fall-out of non-implementation of a decision made by the Department in December, 2002 of
informing HIV positive blood donors about their status.   The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for
having a re-thinking in this regard and not to restrict the revelation  of HIV status to only result seeking donors.   The
Committee emphasizes a dialogue may be initiated   between all stake-holders so as to build up a consensus to include
all donors.  The Department should take action in this regard without any further delay.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1 Tracing Origin of COVID-19 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.1.1   The Committee observes that the origin of the virus still remains obscure and more 
studies need to be conducted to shed light on the origins of the SARS- CoV-2 virus. The 
Committee strongly believes that identification of the true sour ce of the virus is crucial for 
establishment of new zoonotic reservoirs so that future reinfections and diseases in animals as 
well as humans are prevented. Moreover, the information is crucial to reduce any future risks 
due to the emergence and transmissi on of the zoonotic diseases like the recent outbreak of 
Monkeypox.  The Committee is of the opinion that the large scale fatalities and the devastating 
impact of COVID -19 pandemic necessitate the need of being better prepared for possible future 
outbreaks viz the menace and management of Monkeypox. The Committee strongly believes that 
it is incumbent upon global scientists to accelerate its efforts in identifying novel pathogens and 
establish a robust surveillance mechanism for faster detection of the pathogens. In this regard, it 
becomes all the more important to identify the origin of the SARS- CoV-2 virus and investigate its 
origin along all the possible pathway of emergence.  
(Para 1.9 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.1.2  Government of India in 73rd Session of World Health Assembly has already supported the 
proposal to study origins of SARS -CoV-2 virus. Following this, a joint World Health 
Organization (WHO) team of experts that investigated the source of SARS -CoV-2 in January -  
February 2021 concluded that virus probably originated in bats and was introduced in humans 
through an intermediary host species as the most likely pathway and one that will require more 
studies and more specific targeted research. Other hypothesis considered and evaluated by the  
team included possibility of transmission through the trade of frozen cold- chain products. 
Although the investigative team concluded that a laboratory leak is the least likely hypothesis, 
WHO has acknowledged that this still requires further investigation. 
 
1.2 Disease Surveillance System 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.2.1 The Committee takes into account that there is still lack of concrete evidence on whether 
the corona virus reached humans via a laboratory incident. Nevertheless, the Committee 

2 
 
understands that if the origin of corona virus is allowed to remain a mystery, it will have colossal 
consequences over bio- safety and bio- security of the world. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends the Government to reckon its diplomacy to appeal to the comity of nat ions to 
conduct more studies to identify the origin of COVID -19 and penalize the culprits at the 
International platform. The Committee further feels that the increasing number of emerging virus 
highlights the necessity of establishing a robust mechanism for systematic investigation of the 
origin and the route of transmission of the pathogens. The Committee accordingly recommends 
the Ministry to develop a healthcare framework in the country for investigating and managing 
future outbreaks more effectively. In  this regard, the Committee strongly believes that the 
recently constituted Task Force Team led by Dr. VK Paul will track the Monkeypox situation and 
provide guidance to the Government on the expansion of diagnostic facilities in the country and 
combat the menace of Monkeypox.    
(Para 1.10 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.2.2  The recommendation of the Committee has been noted by the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare. It is informed that for strengthening of Disease Surveillance System for 
epidemic prone diseases, to detect and respond to the outbreaks of communicable diseases in the 
country, States/districts have been asked to notify the outbreaks immediately to the 
system. Health officials are required to report the cases of 33 plus communicable diseases 
identified under the programme. This system enables to detect the early warning signals  of 
impending outbreaks ( early rising trends and clustering of cases)  of 33 selected communicable 
diseases, initiation of timely and effective public health actions to reduce mortality and 
morbidity.  
 
1.2.3  Supplemental Information is generated through Media Scanning & Verification Cell 
(MSVC) of Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP)  which is functional at CSU 
(Central Surveillance Unit) at headquarter level and further at state and district level.  It detects 
and shares media alerts with the concerned States/districts for verification and response.  
 
1.2.4  Under IDSP, strengthening of public health labs is also an important component which 
mainly focused on developing lab capacity in India. Public health lab strengthening plan is 
currently based on two strategies:  Strengthening of District public health labs and  Referral lab 
network. 
 
1.2.5  Apart from this, as a long -term goal to better prepare the countr y against public health 
emergencies, PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM -ABHIM) has been 
launched by the Government of India at an outlay of Rs. 64,180 crores with the intent to enhance 
the capacity of primary, secondary and tertiary healt h care facilities and institutes for identifying

1.7 Procurement of Vaccine and its Distribution 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.7.1  The Committee notes that procurement and delivery of vaccines for catering to the 
targeted group of people requires huge amount of financial resources. The Committee observes 
that a robust assessment of the logistic re quirements and streamlining of the procurement 
process is crucial in ensuring the supply chain of the vaccines in the country. As the beginning of 
the National COVID Vaccination Program, much confusion prevailed on the Government's 
vaccine procurement policy. The Committee takes into account that some States raised objection 
to the provision of Liberalized Pricing and Accelerated National COVID -19 Vaccination 
Strategy due to the financial constraints in the procurement of the vaccine that disturbed the 
vaccine demand supply continuum. States complained about acute shortage of vaccines in the 
third phase of vaccination, i.e. 18- 44 age Group while vaccination was the only real weapon or 
the last hope to combat COVID -19. The Committee is of the opinion that the  Centre's erstwhile 
policy of not providing free vaccines to age group of 18- 44 years was devoid of any  justification 
and generated hue and cry amongst vaccine willing citizens.   
(Para 3.10 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.7.2  The COVID -19 vaccination in the country is guided by National Expert Group on 
Vaccine Administration for COVID -19 (NEGVAC) on the basis of concurrent scientific 
evidence. The prioritization for vaccination has been done with an aim to protect the pandemic 
response and health system and to have maximum impact on reduction of disease & deaths due to 
COVID-19. This was later followed by age -based prioritization, which is considered equitable 
and which has also been the practice globally. 
 
1.7.3  Procurement of vaccines was done by al l States/UTs as part of ‘Liberalised Pricing and 
Accelerated National COVID -19 Vaccination Strategy’ that was in effect from 1 st May, 2021 to 
20th June, 2021. A total of 4.57 crore doses were procured by the States/UTs during this period 
through a clear la id down procedure. The demand from private hospitals was collated by states 
and communicated to manufacturers. It is also informed that during this period, Government of 
India continued to supply COVID-19 vaccines free of cost to all States/UTs for priorit y groups of 

7 
 
health care workers, front line workers and persons aged 45 years and above as identified by 
NEGVAC. 
 
1.7.4  Free vaccination to all persons aged 18 years and above started from 21st June 2021. 
 
1.8 Pre-purchase Agreement for Procurement of Vaccine. 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.8.1 The Committee takes note that the Indian Government did not make any upfront payments 
or signed any pre-purchase agreement with the vaccine manufacturers during the developmental 
phase of vaccines. The need of such agreement w as felt when the vaccine supply could not match 
the vaccine demand from the States. The Committee notes that as most of the vaccine centres 
used to get full to its capacity at quick pace, booking a slot on Cowin became herculean task at 
the early stage. Th e Committee is  of the view that the Government should have taken steps to 
enhance vaccine capacity in the country and procure additional vaccine doses. The Committee 
believes that a better assessment of the vaccine requirement in the country could have 
accelerated the vaccination drive. However, absence of a micro -level planning greatly impacted 
the supply chain of vaccines.  
(Para 3.11 of 137th Report) 
Action Taken: 
1.8.2  The issue of vaccine supplies not meeting the vaccine demand was felt across many 
countries of the world. It was because of limited supply of COVID -19 vaccine that an approach 
of vaccinating the most vulnerable population groups was adopted by most countries including 
India. 
 
1.8.3 Vaccination at each CVCs was done based on the laid down SOPs in the operational 
guidelines of COVID -19 vaccination programme. Each vaccinator was allotted a session with 
atleast 100 beneficiary load per day. Number of vaccination sites was planned by States/UTs 
based on their requirements and availability of vaccinators and distribution of vaccines. 
 
1.8.4 Advance information of vaccine allocation to be supplied to the States/UTs was provided 
by the Government of India at the beginning of each month. States/UTs to further plan and 
allocate doses to districts an d vaccination centers. Further, the information about the above 
availability at vaccination center were put in the public domain and widely disseminates it among 
the local population, maximizing the visibility and convenience of citizens. 
 
1.9 Negotiation on Better Price 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.9.1 The Committee further notes that the Procurement Policy was modified from time to time 
to overcome the limitation of each Procurement Process. However, the Committee is of the view 

8 
 
that there exists a huge disparity between the States and many economically weaker States were 
incapable of managing such intricate vaccine logistic requirements on their own.  With the 
change in the guidelines of the procurement policy, the Central Government could negotiate with 
the vaccine manufacturers and settle on a fair and better price. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry to make elaborate arrangements for ensuring procurement in emergency situations.  
(Para 3.12 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.9.2  Vaccine doses provided free o f cost by Government of India are being allocated to 
States/UTs based on criteria such as population, disease burden and the progress of vaccination. 
Further, the Government of India has negotiated with the concerned vaccine manufacturers for 
settling on a  fair and better price and timely production. All efforts were made to ensure timely 
procurement of vaccines during such emergency situations.

Recommendation:

(Para 3.13 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken:

1.11 Modern Technology for Last Mile Delivery of Vaccine 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.11.1  The Committee also notes that in regions with difficult geographical terrain and poor 
connectivity, digitization of vaccine stock inventory and its storage temperature may not be 
possible.  The Committee is concerned especially for States like Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh 

9 
 
and the North Eastern States where road as well as network connectivity is very poor. Ensuring a 
robust vaccine distribution m echanism and monitoring the temperature while ensuring last mile 
delivery of the vaccines may be a challenge in such areas. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Ministry to coordinate with the States and encourage use of modern 
technologies, Drones, Helicopters for the robust distribution of the vaccines.  
(Para 3.27 of 137th Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.11.2    Use of modern technologies like drones, as well as other means i.e. helicopters, boats, 
camel and by foot were used in the Hilly States and NE St ates during the National COVID -19 
Vaccination Programme. However, digitization of vaccine stock inventory through eVIN has 
been rolled out across the country and the States are being supported through PIP for ensuring 
good internet connectivity. 
 
1.12 Indigenous mRNA Vaccine 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.12.1  The Committee observes that the price of Indian vaccines compared to the foreign 
vaccines is less, however, the Committee observes that mRNA vaccines because of their high 
potency have been greatly explored over the conventional vaccine platforms such as subunit, 
killed and live attenuated virus etc. The Committee is given to understand that mRNA vaccines 
provide greater flexibility in comparison to other vaccine platforms. With the virus constantly 
mutating and increasing risk of vaccine escape, mRNA vaccines provide a better alternative and 
more flexibility. The potential for low cost manufacture of the mRNA vaccines is also a major 
advantage. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to explore such versatile 
vaccine platforms in the country and work towards producing cost effective indigenous mRNA 
vaccines.   
(Para 3.32 of 137th Report) 
 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.12.2  
• Noted for compliance.  
• Development of nearly ten COVID -19 vaccine candidates based on about seven different 
platforms has been supported by the Department of Biotechnology. 
• Of these four vaccine candidates received Emergency Use Authorization. These include 
the World’s first DNA vaccine for COVID -19 (ZyCoV-D); and the nations’ first mRNA 
vaccine for COVID-19 (GEMCOVAC-19) stable at 2-80 C. 
 

10 
 
1.13 Research for Booster Doses 
 
Recommendation: 
1.13.1  The Committee notes that Booster or Precautionary doses commenced for all adults at 
Private vaccination Centres from April, 2022. The Committee would l ike to be apprised of the 
evidence based research and the clinical trials conducted in the country that necessitated the 
administering of booster doses in the country. The Committee would like to be informed on the 
reasons for the change in the vaccination policy of the Government and inoculating the citizens 
with the precautionary dose of the same vaccine. The Committee also notes that some reports 
suggest that a booster dose of a vaccine of a different platform could be better than a vaccine of 
the same p latform. The Committee feels that such proposition requires deep research and any 
implementation of such suggestion must be substantiated by in- depth research data, scientific 
interpretations and clinical trials.  
(Para 3.37 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.13.2  A study has been conducted by Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) to examine 
the effect of booster dose of Covaxin which shows increase in the levels of neutralizing 
antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 after the booster dose. The study report can be accessed through 
the given link: https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.01.05.22268777v1. International 
data available on booster doses of AstraZeneca/Covishield suggests 3 -4 times increase in 
neutralizing antibody levels after administration of third dose of AstraZeneca/Covishield.  
 
1.13.3  As per the recommendation of the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization 
(NTAGI), administration of precaution dose has started from 10th January 2022 as a homologous 
precaution dose to Health Care Workers (HCWs), Front Line Workers (FLWs) and persons aged 
60 years who have received two doses of COVID -19 vaccines. This has been subsequently 
expanded to all beneficiaries 18 years and above. 
 
1.14 People Centric Approach 
  
Recommendations: 
 
1.14.1  The Committee is of the view that a robust implementation of the five principles will 
ensure the success of the National Vaccination Program. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry to ensure participation of the key officers from State to the Block level along  with active 
participation of the masses. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to ensure that 
diversion of healthcare forces to manage Covid- related uncertainties must not cause any 
disruption in the delivery of primary health care services. The Comm ittee further recommends 
that that past experiences of universal immunization and elections must be utilized in smooth 

11 
 
implementation of the National Vaccination Program.  At the same time, every effort should be 
made so that there is no compromise on scientific and regulatory rules and norms.  
(Para 4.5 of 137th Report) 
 
Action taken: 
 
1.14.2   The vaccination drive has constantly evolved as per the scientific evidence and ground 
situation of the pandemic, providing the best possible solutions and guidance  for people-centric 
implementation. During the course of time, strategic interventions were instituted to make the 
vaccination program and its process more people centric, convenient and more pragmatic. 
MoHFW has given guidance to the States/UTs on continuing covid vaccination along with 
Primary health services. 
 
1.14.3   The policy decisions and strategic guidance to the vaccination program are guided by the 
expert bodies like NEGVAC, NTAGI and Empowered Groups and Domain Knowledge Experts 
which have stake holders from states/UTs and professional bodies and institutions. The COVID-
19 vaccination utilizes the existing infrastructure of the Universal Immunization Programme 
(UIP), including the cold chain system. Further, all efforts have been made by the Minis try in 
order to ensure that there is no compromise on scientific and regulatory rules and norms.

Recommendation:

"CoWin" to monitor vaccine administration in the country. The Committee notes that a platform 
was crucial for rolling out of the country wide vaccination program and the Co- WIN app formed 
the backbone of the country's vaccination drive. However, some technical  glitches were reported 
in the app and some issues were raised during beneficiary registration on the COWIN App. The 
Committee is of the view that enabling a strong IT framework through Cowin Platform and 
imparting necessary training to all the stakeholder s was crucial for success of the vaccination 
Program.  
(Para 4.24 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.15.2      A unique digital platform - Co-WIN 2.0 supports the vaccination activity, helping the 
beneficiary to register and program officers to tracking of every beneficiary for COVID -19 
vaccination along with real time information on the available stocks of vaccine, their storage 
temperature, actual vaccination process, generation of digital certificates etc. The platform is 
serving as single source of truth for all data related to beneficiaries, vaccination process. 
 

12

portal, across all States and UTs.

1.17 Focus of Vaccination in Rural Areas 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.17.1  The Committee understands that there exists a huge digital divide between the rural and 
the urban population. With poor accessibility and connectivity, many areas of the country still 
remain disconnected from the digital ecosystem. The Committee notes that rural areas tend to be 
neglected as the level of awareness is very poor. The Committee recommends the Ministry to take 
effective measures to ensure that the rural areas especially the tribal areas are also included in 
the vaccination drive. The Committee notes that in the absence of internet connectivity, entering 
data in the app is a challenge. The Committee accordingly, recommends the Ministry to ensure 
that the data collected in the physical form is uploaded in the Cowin app at the earliest. The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry must aim towards an inclusive vaccination policy and 
the vaccination drive must include the marginalized and the vulnerable population of the country 
too.   
(Para 4.26 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.17.2  The registration and vaccination of people without access to digital technology can be 
done through walk- in registration and vaccination of either single individual or groups of 
individuals at COVID -19 Vaccination Centre (CVC),  Facilitated cohort on –site registration and 
vaccination, Assisted registration through Common Service Centers (CSCs) or 1075 

13 
 
helpline/State’s Call Center, Special sessions for people who don’t have any of the specified 
identity cards such as migrants, seers, nomads etc.

1.17.5  A total of 71.7% vaccine doses have been administered in COVID Vaccination Center

1.18 Data on Efficacy of Vaccination 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.18.1  The Committee also notes that through CoWin the Ministry has been successful in 
administering 2 billion COVID doses and CoWin holds a huge repository of the vaccination data. 
However, various stakeholders during the discussion highlighted the absence of any data on the 
efficacy of the vaccine. The Committee accordingly notes that even with an outstanding CoWin 
data system, the country has no extensive records of after immunisation effects in its population. 
The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to facilitate linkages between CoWin and other 
data systems and share the data in the public domain. The Committee is of the opinion that 
building inter -operable data systems that ensure real time data exchange can provide a better 
assessment of the efficacy of the vaccines. The Committee further feels that this digital ecosystem 
can be aptly utilised for not only monitoring the vaccine supply chain but also promoting 
concrete research and formulating better policy decisions.   
(Para 4.27 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.18.2  India COVID-19 Vaccine Tracker has been developed by ICMR by utilising COVID -19 
Vaccination data from Co -WIN Port al & testing data from ICMR portal using a common 
identification to link the two data system. It is analysed by ICMR using common identifier to 
measure Vaccine Effectiveness on Mortality (Person-Time Analysis).

Recommendation: 
 
1.22.1  The Committee is of the firm opinion that India should ensure adequate availability of 
vaccines in the country alongwith expanding its collaboration with other countries under

vaccine equity i.e. global equitable vaccine distribution among the less developed Asian, African 
and Latin American countries.

launched Vaccine Maitri in January 2021. In li ne with our Neighbourhood First  policy, the

Recommendation: 
 
1.24.1 The Committee recommends the Government to lay special e mphasis on the 
strengthening of the end -to-end vaccine supply chain and logistics systems. The Ministry of

1.35 Waiver of Intellectual Property Protection for COVID Vaccines And Other COVID -
19 Diagnostics and Therapeutics 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.35.1 Attention of the Committee has also been drawn to the proposal of temporary waiver of 
Intellectual property protection for COVID vaccines and other COVID -19 diagnostics and 
therapeutics at WTO. The Committee  believes that exclusive control over vaccines via patents 
can pose a hurdle in ensuring vaccine access to countries that lack the vaccine manufacturing 
capacity. The looming fear of future resurgence and more virulent viruses persists and global 
eradication of the COVID is crucial for halting this pandemic. The Committee, therefore, 
believes that transfer of technology and waiver will significantly bridge the large demand supply 
gap as the vaccines will be produced without authorization from the patent hol der. The 
Committee strongly believes that for ensuring vaccine equity, there is a need to expand the 
vaccine manufacturing capacity across the globe and waive the Intellectual Property Protection 
(IPP) for COVID -19 vaccines. This can help countries in scal ing up the production of vaccines 
and make vaccines more affordable and accessible to everyone. The Committee, however, also 
believes that special emphasis will have to be laid on ensuring safety and quality standard for 
mass vaccine manufacturing. The Com mittee further notes that the move to waive Intellectual 
Property Protections (IPP) must not disincentivize the Pharmaceutical companies to invest on 
vaccine research rather the Industry and the countries across the world must unite and work 
together to expand the global vaccine manufacturing  capacity.    
 
1.35.2  The Committee accordingly urges the Government to continue making efforts for waiver 
of IP Protection for COVID vaccines and other COVID -19 diagnostics and therapeutics so that 
the vaccines are p roduced on a large scale and 100% vaccination of the world population is 
achieved.  
(Para 6.27& 6.28 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.35.3  In October 2020, India and South Africa submitted a proposal for a waiver from certain 
provisions of the Trade -Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement for 
the prevention, treatment and containment of COVID -19 to the WTO TRIPS Council. The 
proposal sought a temporary waiver from certain provisions of the TRIPS Agreement relating to 
patents, copyrights, industrial designs and trade secrets to the extent that they pose a barrier to 

25 
 
accessing COVID -19 products and technologies. This proposal was co- sponsored by 65 WTO 
Members and received wide-ranging support from international Organisations, acad emicians and 
world leaders. 
 
1.35.4  As a result of persistent follow up at various levels by India along with co- sponsors of the 
proposal, a decision on this matter was taken during the 12 thMinisterial Conference of the WTO. 
The key features of the outcome of the TRIPS waiver are the following: 
• can only be used by 'eligible Members,' i.e., developing country Members. 
• covers patents for producing and supplying vaccines needed to address the COVID -19 
pandemic. 
• includes some TRIPS -plus elements such as necess ity tests, efforts to  
prevent re-exportation, notification requirements etc. 
• waives the requirement of Article 31(f) of TRIPS and allows the products manufactured 
under the authorization to be exported to eligible Members. 
• requires Members to prevent re -exportation of the products manufactured under the 
authorization. 
• for remuneration, Members are to consider the humanitarian and not -for-profit purpose of 
specific vaccine distribution programs. 
• applicable for five years from the date of the decision. 
• Members have to decide on this Decision's extension to COVID -19 diagnostics and 
therapeutics within six months. 
 
1.35.5  Some of the critical demands of India that this decision be possibly extended to COVID -
19 diagnostics and therapeutics, and applicability of this decision for five years have been 
accepted. India led a global deal on vaccines which may help poor and developing countries to 
get better vaccine access, availability and affordability. 
 
1.35.6  India’s stand was eventually supported by more than 120 Members of the WTO. WTO 
members are currently deliberating the prospect and modalities for extending the TRIPS decision 
to therapeutics and diagnostics at the TRIPS Council. India, along with South Africa, Pakistan, 
Indonesia, Egypt and Tanzania, made a s ubmission before the TRIPS Council on the 
implementation of the TRIPS decision that deals with extending the TRIPS decision to 
therapeutics and diagnostics.

1.42 Need of Change in Vaccination Policy 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.42.1  The Committee is of the opinion that the effectiveness studies of the vaccines on the newer 
variants of the virus should have been conducted by the research bodies in India along with the 
beginning of the vaccination drive.  Countries like US and UK started conducting various studies 
to determine the proportion of people who were vaccinated but still either got severely ill or died 
due to the COVID.  The Committee further notes the research studies that recommended delay in 
the second dose of the AstraZeneca vaccine beyond the earlier recommended 4 weeks.  This was 
also endorsed by the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) 
Committee. In May, 2021, the COVID Working Group chaired by Dr N K Arora also 
recommended extension of the gap between the first and second doses of COVISHIELD vaccine 
to 12-16 weeks. The earlier gap between the two doses of COVISHIELD vaccine was 6 -8 weeks. 
The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Government to find out scienti fically, the 
reasonable gap between the two doses of the vaccine on the gap between the 2 nd and 
precautionary booster dose in the interest of public health otherwise common masses apprehend 
that Government is allowing adjustment of time gap between two dos es of vaccine to clear the 
stock of vaccine manufacturers.   
 (Para 6.42 of 137th Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.42.2  Dose gaps are revised based on the evolving evidences and recommendations of COVID 
working group (of domain knowledge experts), of National Tec hnical Advisory Group on 
Immunization (NTAGI). 
 
1.42.3  Following studies conducted by ICMR and other researchers clearly indicate that6months 
gap between the primary and booster dose is appropriate: 
 
1. Persistence of immunity and impact of third dose of ina ctivated COVID-19 vaccine against 
emerging variants. 
2. Booster dose of the inactivated COVID -19 vaccine BBV152 (Covaxin) enhances the 
neutralizing antibody response against Alpha, Beta, Delta and Omicron variants of concern. 
3. Sub-optimal neutralization of omicron (B.1.1.529) variant by antibodies induced by vaccine 
alone or SARS-CoV-2 Infection plus vaccine (hybrid immunity) post 6-months. 
4. Reduced neutralizing antibody response in naïve Covishield vaccines against Omicron 
emphasizes booster vaccination. 
 
1.43 Research for Optimisation of Vaccine Dosage  
 
Recommendation: 
1.43.1   The Committee feels that with the huge repository of vaccination data in the country, 
India should have been at the forefront of conducting better assessment of the vaccine efficacy in 

31 
 
its population. The Committee believes that any change in the national vaccination policy should 
have been substantiated by real -life evidences and concrete research in the country itself. The

 (Para 6.43 of 137th Report)

1.43.2  Noted for compliance. 
 
1.44 Preparedness of Vaccination Strategies 
 
Recommendation: 
1.44.1  The Committee further recommends that there is a need to develop a mechanism that in 
case of future outbreaks of the pandemic, the research infrastructure is put into action and the 
vaccine policy is accordingly modified for better results. The Committee again emphasizes that 
the preparedness of vaccination strategies requires much more clinical research so that the rapid 
response care strategies are adopted. 
 (Para 6.44 of 137th Report) 
 
Action Taken:

waves. 
 
1.45 Enhancement in the Honorarium of AWWS/AWHS and ASHAS 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.45.1  The Committee applauds the Anganwadi Workers (AWWs), Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) 
and Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHAs) who were  extensively involved in COVID -19 
awareness drive in the community. The Committee notes that ASHAs, AWWs and AWHs acted as 
the frontline workers during the pandemic and were responsible for spreading awareness about 
COVID-19 and safety protocols. The ASHAs were also tasked with identifying as well as tracking 
COVID-19 positive cases and carry ing out vaccination drive. ASHAs, AWWs and AWHs have 
played an important role in community surveillance as has also been applauded by WHO, 
however, these frontline workers remain unrewarded. The Committee accordingly recommends 
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Women and Child Development to 
ensure timely payment of wages along with other social security benefits. The Committee further 

32 
 
recommends the Government to consider incentives and financial protection for the ASHAs,

1.45.2

1.46  Administration of Booster Doses 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.46.1  The Committee notes that administration of free booster doses has enhanced the booster 
dose uptake. However, the Committee notes that this free precautionary  dose window is only for 
75 days. The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to extend the 75 days window and 
make the precautionary dose free for all so that complete vaccination of all can be ensured.  
 (Para 6.53 of 137th Report)

beneficiaries at the COVID vaccination centres. 

33 
 
1.47 Awareness Regarding Precautionary Dosage  
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.47.1  The Committee further notes that the ease of access to vaccination site also has a major 
role to play in increase in vaccination rate. The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to 
increase the Government COVID Vac cination centres across all the States/UTs. The Committee 
is also concerned at the general prevalence of complacency in the healthcare workers as well as 
the public towards booster doses. The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to work 
towards increasing awareness regarding the precautionary dose among the public, particularly 
among the immune-compromised and people with co morbidities.  
 (Para 6.54 of 137th Report)

precaution dose at door step. The campaign contributed in r eaching out to the beneficiary till the 
last mile including the old-aged, differently-abled and even the vaccine hesitant populations. 
 
1.47.3  Further, from 15th July 2022 to 30th   September 2022, as part of the celebration of 75 years 
of India’s Independence, Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav, Government of India launched the ‘COVID 
Vaccination Amrit Mahotsava’ initiative under which free precaution doses were administered to

1.48 Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.48.1  The Committee notes that on 19 th July, 2022, a total of 28 AEFI were reported across the 
country and total AEFI is reported to be 0.006% of the total cases. The C ommittee observes that 
under-reporting and poor quality data collection may be the reason behind reporting of such less 
number of AEFI. However, the Committee takes note of the unusual peak in AEFI on 10 th July, 
2022 where 743 AEFI cases were reported. The  Committee would like to be apprised of the 
reason behind this sudden rise in the cases and the vaccines that caused the adverse reaction.   
 (Para 6.57 of 137th Report) 
 
 

34 
 
Action Taken: 
1.48.2  As per the AEFI guidelines for COVID -19 vaccines, all the adve rse events being entered 
in COWIN are to be verified by the DIO as minor, severe and serious adverse events based on the 
completeness of the information. All cases which are incomplete in nature or have been 
inadvertently entered are then filtered out and the database is updated accordingly. 
 
1.49 Adverse Effects of Vaccination 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.49.1  The Committee notes that mild side effects after administering of the vaccines are usually 
reported as the body requires time to adjust to the vaccination dose. However, the Committee 
feels that the Ministry must ensure that possible adverse effects are communicated to the people 
followed by timely treatment. Attention of the Committee is also brought to the death of a patient 
post COVID -19 vaccination. The C ommittee notes that in the concerned case, the AEFI 
Committee released its assessment Report after almost seven months. The Committee strongly 
recommends the Ministry to ensure that appropriate investigation must be done and AEFI 
Committee must expedite its examination of each adverse cases.   
 (Para 6.58 of 137th Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.49.2  The MOHFW has frequently sent out letters to the states with specific instructions for 
vaccinators to share information on possible side effects of vaccines and spec ific treatment 
guidelines for doctors. An example is the information regarding Thrombosis and 
Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (TTS) following adenovector vaccines. 
1.49.3  The process of causality assessment comprises of different steps starting from reporting 
and completion of investigations by the District AEFI Committee and sharing of all supporting 
documents such as hospital records, post mortem reports, laboratory test reports, etc. to the state 
and the national AEFI committees. The members of the state and national AEFI committee then 
discuss each case in detail, first fixing the diagnosis and then the causality assessment 
classification using standard globally accepted causality assessment guidelines of WHO. 
 
1.50 Liability of Manufacturers on AEFI 
 
Recommendation: 
1.50.1  The Committee also notes that COVID -19 vaccination is voluntary and presently there is 
no mechanism of compensation to beneficiaries or liability of vaccine manufacturer in case of 
any Adverse Event Following Immunization. The Committee, t herefore, strongly recommends the 
Ministry to create a clear framework of vaccine liability for manufacturer in case of AEFI so that 
adequate compensation can be provided to the aggrieved individuals.  
 (Para 6.59 of 137th Report) 
 

35 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.50.2  COVID vaccination is like vaccination under Universal Immunization programme is free 
and voluntary in Government CVCs. The policy of Government of India is  not to award any 
compensation to victims and kin of those who suffer any Adverse Event Following 
Immunization. However free treatment is available at Govt. hospitals and Health facility in case 
of any serious Adverse Event Following Immunization. 
 
1.51 Surveillance of Post COVID Complications 
 
Recommendation: 
 
1.51.1  The Committee also notes the findings of various research studies that have indicated the 
prevalence of long COVID among individuals infected with COVID. Even after the infection has 
passed, individuals have been reported to experience lingering symptoms. The Committee 
observes that there is  a need to monitor and conduct surveillance of post COVID complications. 
The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to frame a 
treatment protocol and make specific guidelines for managing post COVID complications and 
related health problems arising due to the initial infection. The Ministry must also work towards 
sensitizing the Indian Health Public System to deal with such cases of long COVID. The 
Committee further recommends the Ministry to ensure medical support for Long COVID 
sufferers and train the healthcare workers for managing patients with Long COVID.   
 
 (Para 6.60 of 137th Report) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.51.2  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare issued a Comprehensive Guidelines for 
Management of Post -COVID Sequelae on 21 st October 2021 after expert consultations to guide 
doctors on post -COVID-19 complications and their management. These guidelines have been 
widely disseminated and also deliberated upon during clinical webinars held under MoHFW’s 
Centers of Excellen ce initiative through aegis of AIIMS, New Delhi in collaboration with State 
level Centers of Excellence as well as various professional organizations.

development of new drugs especially repurposed Ayush 64 in management of COVID -19. The

scientific research and drug devel opment process entailing pre clinical as well as clinical trials.

ministerial linkages and collaborate with other Departments for undertaking clinical studies on

Recommendation:

integrated health care policy. The Committee accordingly urges the Government to continue
